Video latency affects manual operation. For UI automation, do not rely on fixed sleep timers. Write assertions based on page state, since waiting time is determined by page loading speed, device load and control connection quality.

This lab uses Redroid for the Android runtime and scrcpy to view and control the screen. A browser console, tenant permissions, WebRTC gateway and billing system require extra implementation.

3 Deploying Your First Redroid Instance on a Linux Server

Check the Host Requirements First

Redroid runs on the Linux host kernel. Prepare a Linux host where you can manage kernel modules and run privileged containers, and install Docker Engine. For learning, you can start with 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of RAM, and an SSD. Determine actual capacity through load tests.

Redroid's kernel requirements include Binder, binderfs, ashmem or memfd, and corresponding memory allocation capabilities. The official docs also require a 4 KB page size. Verify these ahead of time, especially on ARM cloud servers. Docker Desktop’s underlying Linux VM must satisfy the same requirements.

Run these checks on your server:

uname -m
uname -r
getconf PAGE_SIZE
docker version

# Load the Binder driver
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

# Check binderfs support
grep -w binder /proc/filesystems

If you get Module binder_linux not found, install the matching kernel modules extra package on Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y "linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)"
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

Package names differ for cloud-customized kernels. Follow Redroid official deployment docs for your distribution. Kernel version alone is not enough to guarantee Android image compatibility.

Create the Container and Persist Its Data

Create a lab directory, save this as start-phone.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

PHONE_NAME="cloudphone-01"
PHONE_PORT="15555"
PHONE_IMAGE="redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest"
PHONE_DATA_DIR="${PWD}/data/${PHONE_NAME}"

mkdir -p "$PHONE_DATA_DIR"
docker pull "$PHONE_IMAGE"

docker run -d \
  --name "$PHONE_NAME" \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --privileged \
  --cpus="2" \
  --memory="3g" \
  -p "127.0.0.1:${PHONE_PORT}:5555" \
  -v "${PHONE_DATA_DIR}:/data" \
  "$PHONE_IMAGE" \
  androidboot.use_memfd=true \
  androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
  androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
  androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
  androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest

docker ps --filter "name=${PHONE_NAME}"

Run it with

bash start-phone.sh

Key parameters explained:

  • /data volume: Persist app data separately for each instance
  • 127.0.0.1:15555:5555: ADB only binds to loopback; use SSH forwarding for remote access
  • guest: Software rendering, good for initial verification
  • --cpus / --memory: Resource limits, tune based on your workload

After first deployment, use these commands to start/restart:

docker start cloudphone-01
docker restart cloudphone-01

Once validated, pin the image digest to avoid unexpected updates:

docker image inspect redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
  --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'

Connect Through ADB and Confirm Android Has Finished Booting

Install platform tools:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y adb python3 python3-venv

python3 --version
adb version
adb start-server
adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
adb devices -l

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.build.version.release
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist

Important: adb devices only confirms ADB transport. Wait for sys.boot_completed=1 before running automation.

Access the Server Instance from Your Local Computer

Start SSH port forwarding (keep this terminal open):

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  your_user@your_server

Then connect locally and view screen with scrcpy:

adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
scrcpy -s 127.0.0.1:15555 --max-size=1024 --max-fps=15

4 Organizing ADB Commands into a Reusable Python Module

Save as adbkit.py

from pathlib import Path
import shlex
import subprocess
import time

def run_adb(*args: str, serial: str | None = None,
            timeout: float = 15) -> bytes:
    command = ["adb"]
    if serial is not None:
        command.extend(["-s", serial])
    command.extend(args)

    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            command,
            capture_output=True,
            timeout=timeout,
            check=False,
        )
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
        raise TimeoutError(f"ADB command exceeded {timeout:.1f} seconds") from exc

    if result.returncode != 0:
        message = (result.stderr or result.stdout).decode(
            "utf-8", errors="replace"
        ).strip()
        raise RuntimeError(message[:2000] or "ADB command failed")
    return result.stdout

class Device:
    def __init__(self, serial: str):
        self.serial = serial

    def shell(self, *args: str, timeout: float = 15) -> str:
        output = run_adb(
            "shell", shlex.join(args),
            serial=self.serial, timeout=timeout,
        )
        return output.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip()

    def wait_ready(self, timeout: float = 120) -> None:
        deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
        last_error = "Android is booting"

        def remaining() -> float:
            seconds = deadline - time.monotonic()
            if seconds <= 0:
                raise TimeoutError("Device wait time exhausted")
            return min(10, seconds)

        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            try:
                run_adb("connect", self.serial, timeout=remaining())
                state = run_adb(
                    "get-state", serial=self.serial,
                    timeout=remaining(),
                ).decode().strip()
                booted = self.shell(
                    "getprop", "sys.boot_completed",
                    timeout=remaining(),
                )
                if state == "device" and booted == "1":
                    return
                last_error = f"state={state}, boot_completed={booted!r}"
            except (RuntimeError, TimeoutError) as exc:
                last_error = str(exc)

            time.sleep(max(0, min(2, deadline - time.monotonic())))

        raise TimeoutError(f"Boot wait timed out for {self.serial}, {last_error}")

    def screenshot(self, destination: Path) -> None:
        png = run_adb(
            "exec-out", "screencap", "-p",
            serial=self.serial, timeout=20,
        )
        if not png.startswith(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"):
            raise RuntimeError("Device returned an invalid PNG screenshot")
        destination.write_bytes(png)

This module handles connection retries, boot waiting, timeouts, and binary-safe screenshot capture.

5 Validating a Single Device Before Scaling to Multiple Devices

Save as fleet.py

import argparse
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from datetime import datetime
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import time
from uuid import uuid4

from adbkit import Device, run_adb

def inspect_one(serial: str, output_dir: Path) -> dict:
    started = time.monotonic()
    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    device = Device(serial)
    result = {
        "serial": serial,
        "ok": False,
        "artifacts": str(output_dir),
    }

    try:
        device.wait_ready(timeout=120)
        package_path = device.shell("pm", "path", "com.android.settings")
        if not package_path.startswith("package:"):
            raise RuntimeError("Image is missing com.android.settings")

        launch_output = device.shell(
            "am", "start", "-W", "-a", "android.settings.SETTINGS",
            timeout=30,
        )
        if "Error:" in launch_output:
            raise RuntimeError(launch_output)
        device.shell("pidof", "com.android.settings")
        device.screenshot(output_dir / "screen.png")
        result["ok"] = True
    except Exception as exc:
        result["error"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        capture_errors = []
        try:
            device.screenshot(output_dir / "failure.png")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Screenshot collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        try:
            logs = device.shell(
                "logcat", "-d", "-t", "200", timeout=15,
            )
            (output_dir / "logcat.txt").write_text(logs, encoding="utf-8")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Log collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        result["capture_errors"] = capture_errors

    result["elapsed_seconds"] = round(time.monotonic() - started, 2)
    return result

def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Concurrent Android device health checks")
    parser.add_argument("--serials", nargs="+", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=2)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.workers < 1:
        parser.error("--workers must be greater than 0")

    serials = list(dict.fromkeys(args.serials))
    run_adb("start-server", timeout=20)
    run_name = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    run_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"{run_name}_{uuid4().hex[:8]}"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    results = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=min(args.workers, len(serials))) as pool:
        futures = {}
        for index, serial in enumerate(serials, start=1):
            safe_name = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9_.-]", "_", serial)[:80]
            device_dir = run_dir / f"{index:03d}_{safe_name}"
            future = pool.submit(inspect_one, serial, device_dir)
            futures[future] = serial

        for future in as_completed(futures):
            serial = futures[future]
            try:
                result = future.result()
            except Exception as exc:
                result = {
                    "serial": serial,
                    "ok": False,
                    "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                }
            results.append(result)
            with (run_dir / "results.jsonl").open("a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                file.write(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False), flush=True)

    results.sort(key=lambda item: item["serial"])
    (run_dir / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(results, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8",
    )
    succeeded = sum(item["ok"] for item in results)
    print(f"Checks complete, {succeeded}/{len(results)} succeeded, artifacts in {run_dir}")
    return 0 if succeeded == len(results) else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Test single device:

python3 fleet.py --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 --workers 1

Add Two Instances and Run Checks Concurrently

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

for index in 2 3; do
  name="$(printf 'cloudphone-%02d' "$index")"
  port="$((15554 + index))"
  data_dir="${PWD}/data/${name}"
  mkdir -p "$data_dir"

  docker run -d \
    --name "$name" \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    --privileged \
    --cpus="2" \
    --memory="3g" \
    -p "127.0.0.1:${port}:5555" \
    -v "${data_dir}:/data" \
    redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
    androidboot.use_memfd=true \
    androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
    androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
    androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
    androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest
done

Forward multiple ports locally:

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15556:127.0.0.1:15556 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15557:127.0.0.1:15557 \
  your_user@your_server

Run concurrent health check:

python3 fleet.py \
  --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 127.0.0.1:15556 127.0.0.1:15557 \
  --workers 2

Important: At scale, add device lease / distributed lock to avoid race conditions.

6 Writing UI-Level Business Workflows with uiautomator2

Install dependencies:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install 'uiautomator2>=3,<4' requests
python -m uiautomator2 version

Dump UI hierarchy:

from pathlib import Path
import uiautomator2 as u2

device = u2.connect("127.0.0.1:15555")
Path("hierarchy.xml").write_text(device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8")
device.screenshot("current-screen.png")
print("Saved hierarchy.xml and current-screen.png")

Save login workflow as login.py

import argparse
from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import uiautomator2 as u2

from adbkit import Device

def login(serial: str, package: str, account: str, password: str) -> None:
    Device(serial).wait_ready(timeout=120)
    device = u2.connect(serial)
    device.implicitly_wait(10)
    artifact_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"login_{uuid4().hex}"
    artifact_dir.mkdir(parents=True)

    try:
        device.app_start(package, stop=True)
        username_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/username")
        password_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/password")
        login_button = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/login")

        if not username_field.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Login page loading timed out")

        username_field.set_text(account)
        password_field.set_text(password)
        login_button.click()

        home = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/home_title")
        if not home.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Expected home-page control did not appear after login submission")

        print(f"[{serial}] Post-login page assertion passed")
    except Exception:
        try:
            device.screenshot(str(artifact_dir / "failure.png"))
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to capture failure screenshot, {exc}")
        try:
            (artifact_dir / "hierarchy.xml").write_text(
                device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8",
            )
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to collect UI hierarchy, {exc}")
        raise

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--serial", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--package", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    account = input("Test account ").strip()
    password = getpass("Test password ")
    login(args.serial, package, account, password)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run:

python login.py --serial 127.0.0.1:15555 --package com.example.demo

7 Keeping a Clear Device Model When Integrating a Provider's OpenAPI

Save as cloud_api.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
import os

import requests

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CloudPhone:
    instance_id: str
    serial: str

class ExampleCloudClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, session: requests.Session):
        if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
            raise ValueError("OpenAPI URL must use HTTPS")
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = session

    def list_running(self, max_pages: int = 100) -> list[CloudPhone]:
        phones = {}
        for page in range(1, max_pages + 1):
            response = self.session.get(
                f"{self.base_url}/v1/instances",
                params={"page": page, "page_size": 50},
                timeout=(5, 20),
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            payload = response.json()
            items = payload["items"]
            has_more = payload["has_more"]
            if not isinstance(items, list) or not isinstance(has_more, bool):
                raise ValueError("Invalid instance list response format")

            for item in items:
                if item["status"] == "RUNNING" and item.get("adb_endpoint"):
                    phone = CloudPhone(
                        instance_id=item["id"], serial=item["adb_endpoint"],
                    )
                    phones[phone.instance_id] = phone

            if not has_more:
                return list(phones.values())

        raise RuntimeError("Pagination limit exceeded, check the API pagination contract")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with requests.Session() as session:
        session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {os.environ['CLOUD_API_KEY']}"
        client = ExampleCloudClient(os.environ["CLOUD_API_URL"], session)
        phones = client.list_running()
        print(f"Retrieved {len(phones)} running instances")

Best practice: Isolate provider API logic into this layer, keep your core automation code unchanged.

8 Troubleshooting Along the Pipeline

Symptom Check first Diagnostic steps
Container exits after starting Kernel capabilities, image arch, memory limits docker logs cloudphone-01
ADB connection refused Container status, port mapping, SSH forward docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
ADB online but app won’t launch Boot status, package name getprop sys.boot_completed + pm path
APK install ABI error APK native libs vs image ABI getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist
UI element never found Current page, dialogs, custom view Save screenshot + dump_hierarchy()
Timeouts spike under concurrency Host load, memory, I/O docker stats --no-stream

Common debug commands:

docker logs --tail 100 cloudphone-01
docker inspect cloudphone-01 --format '{{json .State}}'
docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
docker stats --no-stream

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell pm path com.android.settings
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell logcat -d -t 200

9 Choosing Between Self-Hosting and Managed Services

Self-host Redroid gives you full control over images and access, but you take responsibility for kernel compatibility, capacity planning and failure recovery. Managed cloud phones offload infrastructure work, and you evaluate reliability, API, cost and data isolation.

Evaluate with these dimensions:

  • App compatibility: Android version, ABI, GPU, required system services
  • Automation access: ADB auth, credential TTL, rate limits, async task API
  • Batch management: Bulk APK install, instance grouping, permission
  • Continuous operation: Success rate, recovery time under load
  • Data & cost: Isolation, backup, storage / traffic billing

Final Thoughts

After finishing this lab, you get persistent Android instances, ADB access, and batch health check scripts that capture screenshots and logs on failure.

When scaling, define business assertions first, then add task queues, device leases and failure recovery. Reliable large-scale automation is not about clicking, it is about verifying device state and preserving failure evidence.

title: AI-Generated Playwright Tools: 1 in 4 Runs Returned Wrong Data With No Error
description:
Tools that turn a website into an API for an AI agent often generate Playwright code and repair it when it fails. On a recent Launch HN thread, commenters asked two questions about this: can a tool return success when the action never completed, and does anything notice when a field goes empty while the response still looks fine?

I measured it. I changed an orders page in 10 ways and ran 3 AI-generated tools against the baseline and each changed version, with a repair loop. In 16 of 66 runs (16 of the 60 on a changed page) the tool returned wrong data and reported success. The repair loop never saw those runs, because it only starts on an error. A schema check plus four checks against the page turned all 16 into errors, and the repair loop could then work on them.

The code, every generated tool and every run are in the PoC repo.

The setup

The site is a small orders page: 12 orders, 8 of them open, with a Cancel button on each row. The page loads its data from an API. There is a baseline version and 10 changed versions:

Change What the page or API does
css-rename every class and container id renamed
column-swap Customer and Total columns swapped
locale-format totals shown as 1.234,50 € in place of €1,234.50
api-rename the API field total renamed to amount; the page shows —
late-rows the API answers after 2.5 s; placeholder rows until then
paginated 5 orders per page, with a Next page button
soft-error HTTP 200, an error banner, no rows
cancel-409 the cancel API refuses with 409, but the page still says "Order cancelled"
cancel-confirm Cancel opens a confirm dialog
card-layout cards in place of the table

Each tool has two tasks: list the open orders (id, customer, total), and cancel order A-1003.

  • Generation: claude -p --model sonnet writes the tool from the rendered HTML of the baseline page. I did this 3 times, so there are 3 different tools. The model gets the task prompt and the HTML: no tools, no project files, no CLAUDE.md.
  • Repair: when a run fails with an error, the model gets the error, the code and the HTML of the changed page, and writes a new version. Up to 2 repairs per run.
  • Scoring: each run is checked against the server's data. Correct, loud (an error), or silent (no error, wrong result). For the error banner and the refused cancel, an error is the correct result.

The results

Arm Runs Correct Loud Silent
Generated, with repair 66 45 5 16
+ schema check 66 46 7 13
+ checks against the page 66 58 8 0

66 runs per arm: 3 tools, the baseline plus 10 changes, 2 tasks. The repair loop worked when it got an error: in the first arm, all 16 repaired runs ended correct or with an error, never silent. What it never got was the 16 silent runs.

What the silent runs returned

Change Silent (of 3) What the tool returned
locale-format 3 1.234,50 € read as 1.2345, 420,00 € as 42000
cancel-409 3 cancelled: true, but the order is still open
api-rename 3 every total 0
late-rows 2 an empty list
soft-error 2 an empty list
card-layout 2 an empty list
css-rename 1 an empty list

Most come from a line that turns a failure into a value. These two are from the third generated tool:

return Number.isNaN(n) ? 0 : n;                                       // a missing total becomes 0
await page.waitForSelector(ROW, { timeout: 10000 }).catch(() => {});  // a timeout becomes an empty list

The other two tools got the totals of 0 another way: they strip — to an empty string, and Number("") is 0.

All 3 money parsers removed the commas before they parsed the number, so the German format lost its decimal point. All 3 cancels counted as done when the row left the page. On cancel-409 the page removes the row even though the server refused, so each tool saw what it expected.

The common thread is code that prefers a value to an error, and a repair loop that waits for an error never sees it.

What caught them

A schema check on the output (id and customer not empty, total a positive number) caught the 3 runs with totals of 0, and nothing else. An empty list is a valid list. 1.2345 is a positive number.

Four checks against the page, run after the schema, caught the other 13:

  1. The page shows no error banner (role="alert").
  2. The page's "N open orders" count equals the number of orders the tool returned.
  3. The digits of each total match the digits in that row on the page.
  4. After a cancel, a reload shows one open order less, and no row for that id.

With the schema and these checks, no run was silent. Of the 16 runs that had been silent:

  • 8 were repaired to the correct result (locale-format 3, late-rows 2, card-layout 2, css-rename 1).
  • 5 ended with an error, which is the correct result for the error banner and the refused cancel.
  • 3 (api-rename) still failed after 2 repairs, with an error.

Across the arm, 27 runs needed a repair: 19 ended correct and 8 ended with an error (api-rename 3, cancel on the error page 3, cancel with late rows 2).

One check was wrong. On api-rename, two repaired tools read the correct totals from the API, but the page shows —, so check 3 failed them. I count those as errors, not as silent failures.

The limits

  • I wrote the checks after I saw which runs failed silently in the first two arms. They check general things (an error on the page, a count, the digits, a re-read after an action), but they know this page's count label and row markup. Another site needs its own.
  • Three tools from one model, two tasks, one small page. The rates are for this setup, not for any product.
  • The changes are mine, and all of them at once is not how a real site changes.
  • The generated code is saved, so a re-run gives the same numbers. A new generation can give different code.

The repo also has a hand-written tool with Playwright assertions. It had no silent failures in 22 runs, but I wrote it knowing the changes, so it is not a fair comparison.

What I'd do with it

  • If a tool repairs itself on errors, check that it fails when it should. Count the silent results, not the repairs.
  • Search the generated code for lines that turn an error into a value. In these tools: .catch(() => {}) on a wait, isNaN(n) ? 0 : n, and Number() on text that can be empty.
  • Add at least one check that comes from the page and not from the tool: a count the page shows, or a re-read after an action.
  • Treat a schema check as the floor. It catches missing values, not wrong ones.

Repo: qa-gary-parker/poc-ai-tool-silent-failures. The self-healing tests experiment and the mutation testing experiment look at the same problem from the test side. More are in the playbook.

Originally published at https://garyparker.dev/blog/ai-generated-playwright-tools-silent-failures

title: Four Image Models in One Graph: 2512 vs Flux 2 vs Z-Image vs Klein
description:
A 146-node comparison graph with four model families in it. That is a lot of graph, and it is the right shape for the question: which image model should this project use?

What is in the graph

Node Value
UNETLoader qwen_image_2512_bf16.safetensors
CLIPLoader qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors, type qwen_image
VAELoader qwen_image_vae.safetensors
EmptySD3LatentImage 1328 × 1328
EmptyFlux2LatentImage 1248 × 832
KSamplerSelect euler

Plus Flux 2, Z-Image and Klein branches in the same file.

Previews wipes 146 nodes clean

The point of a single graph containing four models is that everything shared — prompt, seed, sampler settings, output naming — is genuinely shared. Four separate graphs would mean four places to make the same mistake.

When you are comparing model families, that matters enormously. A difference you observe could be the model, or it could be a setting you changed in one graph and forgot in another. One graph removes that possibility.

1328 × 1328 versus 1248 × 832

Two different latent geometries for two different families:

  • 1328×1328 (1.76 MP) for the Qwen 2512 path — square
  • 1248×832 (1.04 MP) for the Flux 2 path — 3:2 landscape

Comparing models at different resolutions and different aspects is not a clean comparison. It is, however, how these models are typically used: each has a resolution it does well at, and forcing a common resolution would penalise one.

The honest framing: this compares production configurations, not bare models.

The euler sampler

Plain euler across the board. Deterministic, which is right for a comparison — an ancestral sampler would add noise per step and make two runs of the same model differ.

What a four-model comparison can and cannot tell you

It can tell you: which model produces a result closest to what you want for this prompt, at its natural resolution, with its natural settings.

It cannot tell you: which model is better in general. A different prompt can reverse the ranking. Four models at three aspect ratios and two resolutions is four different experiments wearing one graph.

Practical use

Use it as a screening tool, not a verdict. Run your actual prompt through all four, look at which two are closest, then do a focused comparison between those two at matched settings.

That two-stage approach is much more informative than trying to rank four models from one comparison. The first stage answers "which direction is right", the second answers "which is better".

Where this breaks

  1. Different aspect and resolution per branch makes it a configuration comparison.
  2. 146 nodes is hard to verify — a mis-wired branch produces a plausible image from the wrong model.
  3. Model availability. Four families means four large downloads; a partial setup will produce errors in one branch that look like model failure.
  4. One prompt. Ranking is prompt-specific.

Practical order

Before running: confirm all four model families are actually present on disk. Then run one prompt and check that all four outputs are visibly different — if two look identical, a branch is mis-wired.

Files

https://huggingface.co/AI-KSK/ksk-video-161-comfyui-workflows

Notes

  • Workflow file only. Model weights are not included; each keeps its own licence.
  • Tutorial export, not a product.
  • Node count and latent geometries quoted above are read from the published JSON file.
  • Independent AI-KSK release. Not affiliated with any of the model authors or RunningHub.

title: Your coding agent doesn't need more MCP tools. It needs a map.
description:
The MCP conversation on DEV this month has been great. "MCP Is Dead Simple. And That's Exactly the Problem" and "MCP Token Cost: I Cut My MCP Server From 15 Tools to 4" both land on the same point: MCP is easy to add, and that's exactly how your context window disappears.

I agree. And I think there's a second half to it that we don't talk about enough.

Even with a lean tool list, a coding agent still burns most of its context on one thing: finding its way around your code. Grep, open a file, grep again, open three more. More tools don't fix that. A map does.

I work on Graphify, so I have a horse in this race. But the numbers below are from my own terminal, and you can rerun every one of them.

Two places your tokens go

1. Tool definitions. Every tool schema sits in context on every turn, whether the agent uses it or not. The 15-tools-to-4 post cites GitHub's official MCP server at about 55,000 tokens across 93 tool definitions before you ask a single question. Stack five or six servers like that and you've spent a big slice of the window on menus.

2. Navigation. This one is sneakier. The agent asks "who calls this function?" and the only way it knows to answer is to search text and read files. Files are big. The answer is small.

Most of the advice so far targets the first problem: fewer, sharper tools. That's right. Here's what happens when you also go after the second one.

The experiment: one question, two ways

Repo: Click, the Python CLI library, at commit 8abb77a. Question: "What calls make_context, and what does it call?" Token counts use OpenAI's o200k_base tokenizer via tiktoken.

Way 1: grep and read 

grep -rn make_context --include='*.py' --include='*.md' .

12 matches across 5 files. The grep output itself is tiny, about 257 tokens. But matches aren't answers. Grep tells you where the string appears, not who calls whom. So the agent opens the files to figure it out.

Those 5 files add up to about 48,900 tokens. src/click/core.py alone is about 33,600.

Way 2: ask the graph

I built a graph of the same repo once (graphify update ., about 3 seconds, no LLM, no embeddings) and served it over MCP with graphify-mcp. Then one tool call:

{ "tool": "get_neighbors", "arguments": { "label": "make_context" } }

Neighbors of .make_context():
  --> .parse_args() [calls] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1389
  --> Any [references] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1355
  --> Context [references] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1355
  <-- .main() [calls] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1584
  <-- Command [method] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1355
  <-- This function when given an info name and arguments will kick off the parsing… [rationale_for] [EXTRACTED] at=src/click/core.py:L1362
  <-- _resolve_context() [calls] [INFERRED 0.85] at=src/click/shell_completion.py:L706

That's about 188 tokens. Callers, callees, file and line for each, and a tag on every edge: EXTRACTED means read straight from the source, INFERRED means resolved by Graphify with a confidence score.

It even caught the cross-file caller, _resolve_context() in shell_completion.py. That's the one you'd miss if you only opened core.py.

The scoreboard

Grep + read Code graph over MCP
Calls to answer 1 search + up to 5 file reads 1
Tokens in context ~257 search + ~48,900 files ~188
Says who calls whom You work it out Yes, with direction
File and line per hop From grep only Yes

And the tool menu that makes this possible? graphify-mcp exposes 10 tools. I dumped their names, descriptions and input schemas from the server: about 1,600 tokens total.

So what does "a map" actually mean?

Not a bigger prompt. Not a CLAUDE.md that goes stale. A structure the agent can query:

  • Nodes for functions, classes, modules and docs
  • Edges for calls, imports, references and inheritance
  • Communities that roughly match your subsystems (Click has 213)
  • Freshness baked in. graph_stats on Click ends with Built at commit: 8abb77a… (matches HEAD), so the agent knows the map matches the code.

Once that exists, a lot of questions collapse into one call:

  • "Who calls this?" → get_neighbors
  • "How does A reach B?" → shortest_path
  • "What's the core of this repo?" → god_nodes
  • "Give me just enough context for this question" → query_graph, which stays inside a token budget (2,000 by default)

That's the same lesson as the lean-tools posts, applied to the codebase instead of the API: give the model fewer, better-shaped things to look at.

Try it on your repo (5 minutes) 

pip install "graphifyy[mcp]"
cd your-repo && graphify update .
claude mcp add --transport stdio graphify -- graphify-mcp "$(pwd)/graphify-out/graph.json"

Cursor and other JSON clients work too. The MCP server docs have every config. If you'd rather not run anything locally, hosted Graphify indexes your GitHub repos and keeps the graph fresh, and it connects to Claude Code with one command.

If this was useful, a ⭐ on GitHub genuinely helps.

Your turn

I'm curious where everyone's tokens actually go.

When you look at a long agent session, what eats more of your context: tool definitions, or the agent reading files to find its way around? Drop your numbers or your gut feel in the comments. I'll rerun this experiment on any public repo you name.

title: AnyLight: Letting Blender's Physical Renderer Decide the Lighting
description:
AI lighting is a lottery. Ask for a specific light direction and the model gives you something plausible, not something specific. AnyLight replaces that guess with an actual physics render: build the light in 3D, render a reference, and let the AI model match it.

The graph

Node Value
UNETLoader qwen_image_edit_2511_bf16.safetensors
CLIPLoader qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors, type qwen_image
VAELoader qwen_image_vae.safetensors
LoraLoaderModelOnly Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Lightning-8steps-V1.0-fp32 at 1.0
EmptySD3LatentImage 928 × 1664

62 nodes.

fp32 rather than bf16

The Lightning LoRA is loaded as fp32, not the bf16 used in other releases.

That is a notable choice for a distillation LoRA. FP32 is twice the memory of BF16 for this component, and the only reason to accept that is if the reduced precision measurably changed behaviour. For a lighting-control task where subtle gradients matter, that is plausible.

If you have memory pressure, BF16 is the first downgrade to try — but expect a difference, not equivalence.

Eight steps, not four

Lightning-8steps-V1.0 — eight steps, versus the four-step Lightning variants elsewhere.

Eight steps for a lighting edit makes sense: the task requires redistributing shading across every surface in the image, which is a global operation. Four steps cannot converge on a global change without visible banding.

What AnyLight actually does

The idea is to use Blender's renderer as the source of truth for lighting:

  1. Build a rough 3D scene matching the image's geometry
  2. Place lights physically
  3. Render
  4. Use the render as a lighting reference for the AI model

The AI model then has an unambiguous target: light from this direction, this intensity, this colour, with these shadows. No prompt guessing.

That is why the title claims an end to randomness. The claim is structural, not a quality claim about the model.

The cost

Building a 3D scene that matches an image's geometry is real work. For a simple object on a table it is minutes. For a person in a complex environment it is an afternoon.

So the technique pays off when:

  • The lighting must be exactly right
  • Multiple images need consistent lighting
  • The scene geometry is simple enough to model quickly

And it does not pay off for one-off images with forgiving requirements.

Where this breaks

  1. Geometry mismatch. If the 3D scene's proportions differ from the image, the shadows land in the wrong places and the model produces something incoherent.
  2. Occlusion. The release claims complex occlusion works; that depends entirely on modelling it in 3D first.
  3. 928 × 1664 is fixed — other aspects get implicit cropping.
  4. fp32 LoRA costs memory.
  5. 62 nodes plus a 3D scene is a heavy setup for a lighting change.

Practical approach

Start with a simple scene — an object on a surface with one light. Confirm the pipeline works and the shadow direction matches your Blender render. Then increase complexity. The first attempt on a person in a room will fail for geometry reasons, not AI reasons, and that is easier to diagnose on a simple scene.

Workflows

One graph, published on RunningHub with invite code rh-v1111: AnyLight lighting control with Qwen 2511.

  • Node count and loader values quoted above are read from the published JSON file.

title: Building Production-Grade AI Agents: How I Designed an Autonomous Refund System with Google ADK, HITL Guardrails & Zero Hallucination
description:
Series Navigation:

  • Part 1 (Foundations): Mastering Google ADK: From Zero to Tool-Driven AI Agents
  • Part 2 (This Post): Deep-Dive Architecture, Design Philosophy, End-to-End Flow & System Design
  • GitHub Reference Repo: github.com/gouravchawla334/adk-refund-agent

In Part 1, I explored why Google ADK shifts agent development from fragile prompt-chaining to deterministic software engineering. In this post, I want to pull back the curtain on adk-refund-agent—walking through my exact engineering thought process, features, system design concepts, and how I achieved zero hallucination, strict HITL gates, and robust cost savings.

1. The Core Design Philosophy: Why "Tool-Only" & "Guardrail-First"?

When I set out to build a customer support agent, the most common pitfall I wanted to avoid was giving an LLM a massive system prompt containing return policies and letting it calculate refunds conversationally. In production finance workflows, that approach fails for three distinct reasons:

  1. LLMs are probabilistic, not calculators: Asking an LLM to subtract a 10% restocking fee from an order subtotal while conditionally waiving it for defective items will eventually result in a hallucinated dollar figure.
  2. Prompts are not security boundaries: Telling an LLM "Never refund more than $150" in a system prompt can easily be bypassed via prompt injection. True security must live in deterministic code (before_tool_callback), never in prompt text.
  3. Blind automation destroys user trust: An autonomous agent shouldn't silently yank money or process a return before confirming what item is being returned and why.

My Architectural Thesis

I designed RefundOrchestratorAgent around a strict separation of concerns:

  • The LLM (gemini-2.5-flash) is purely a semantic router and conversational translator. It understands user intent, invokes tools, and translates structured JSON results into concise plain English.
  • Python tools own 100% of state, math, and mutations. Every database lookup, fee deduction, and payment gateway call happens inside isolated, unit-tested Python functions.
  • ADK Lifecycle Callbacks act as a deterministic Policy Plane. Code intercepts every model request and tool call before execution to enforce authorization, sequence order, financial caps, and token budgets.

2. End-to-End Execution Flow & Interactive HITL Gates

Rather than executing an entire refund in one opaque step, I designed the agent to guide the customer through five explicit stages punctuated by Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) confirmation gates:

[User: "I want a refund"]
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STAGE 1: Intake & SQL-Safe Lookup                                       │
│ • Prompt for Order ID (ORD-XXXXX)                                       │
│ • Validate regex ^ORD-[0-9]{5}$ -> Query SQLite via parameterized SQL   │
│ • [If missing/invalid] ──► Plain-English "Order not available" & STOP   │
└────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STAGE 2: HITL Confirmation Gate #1 (Order Summary & Return Reason)      │
│ • Summarize items & paid amount in plain English                        │
│ • Ask WHY the customer is returning the item                            │
│ • Call capture_return_feedback(order_id, reason_category, comment)      │
└────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STAGE 3: Parallel Validation & Risk Plane                               │
│ • get_return_logistics(order_id)   ──► Verify DELIVERED_AT_WAREHOUSE    │
│ • fetch_refund_policy(category_id) ──► Get return window & fee %        │
│ • check_fraud_score(cust_id, oid)  ──► Evaluate velocity risk           │
│ • [If not scanned at warehouse] ──► Plain-English hold message & STOP   │
└────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STAGE 4: Deterministic Math & HITL Confirmation Gate #2                 │
│ • calculate_refund_amount() computes subtotal, fees & net payout        │
│ • Present exact breakdown & ask explicit confirmation ("Yes / Confirm") │
└────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STAGE 5: Conditional Execution vs. Finance Escalation                   │
│ • before_tool_callback checks: amount <= $150.00 AND fraud_flagged=False│
│   ├──► PASS: Inject verified amount + idempotency_key ──► Payout!       │
│   └──► FAIL: Block payout ──► create_hitl_ticket() for Finance Queue    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

3. Project Features & System Design Implementations

To make this agent robust enough for real-world production, I integrated several key system design patterns and safeguards:

A. Eradicating Hallucinations (Zero-Math LLM Policy)

  • The Design: The LLM is strictly banned from performing arithmetic. All calculations—including subtotals, restocking fee deductions, and shipping reimbursements—happen inside calculate_refund_amount().
  • State Locking: When the calculation tool runs, after_tool_callback captures the verified net_refund_amount and stores it securely in tool_context.state["verified_refund_amount"]. When execute_payment_refund is eventually called, before_tool_callback overwrites any amount the LLM passed and injects the verified state value directly. The model cannot alter a single cent.

B. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Gateways

  • Gate #1 (Context & Feedback): Before checking warehouse logs or policies, the agent summarizes the fetched order details in plain English and asks the customer for their return reason. This ensures the customer agrees on which item is being evaluated.
  • Gate #2 (Financial Confirmation): After deterministic math runs, the agent presents the exact itemized breakdown and waits for explicit user consent ("Yes", "Confirm") before authorizing any financial mutation.
  • Gate #3 (Automatic Escalation): If a refund exceeds my auto-approval threshold of $150.00 or triggers fraud velocity flags, before_tool_callback intercepts the payout tool, blocks it entirely, and routes the order to a manual finance review queue via create_hitl_ticket().

C. Cost Optimization & Token Efficiency

  • Token Capping: I configured max_output_tokens=300 and temperature=0.0 in GenerateContentConfig to prevent runaway verbose responses and keep API latency low.
  • Prompt Caching Optimization: My prompts.py file is kept 100% static (free of dynamic timestamps or user identifiers), maximizing Gemini's prompt caching hit rate across sessions.
  • Payload Pruning: In after_tool_callback, I prune verbose internal database metadata (such as raw database timestamps and audit logs) from get_order_details before the response enters the LLM context window. This drastically reduces token bloat over multi-turn conversations.

D. Security & Threat Mitigation (SQL Injection & Domain Locking)

  • SQL Injection Defense: Incoming order IDs are validated against a strict regular expression (^ORD-[0-9]{5}$) via Pydantic input validators before touching the database. Furthermore, all database operations use strictly parameterized queries (? bindings) rather than raw string formatting.
  • Strict Domain Locking: To prevent prompt hijacking or off-topic chat (e.g., asking the agent to write code or tell jokes), my before_model_callback intercepts irrelevant queries instantly and responds with a rigid deflection message: "I am a refund agent only and can only help you process returns and refunds."
  • Anti-Looping Guardrail: I track consecutive identical assistant replies in tool_context.state. If the agent repeats the same clarifying question twice, it stops looping and outputs a polite troubleshooting fallback.

4. Local Database & Test Scenarios

To make the repository testable offline in seconds without cloud dependencies, I built refund_agent/db.py to initialize a local SQLite database (local_refund_store.db) seeded with three test cases:

  1. ORD-98765 (Happy Path Auto-Approval):
  2. Data: Apparel order ($90.00 items + $10.00 shipping = $100.00), scanned at warehouse (DELIVERED_AT_WAREHOUSE).

  3. Behavior: If returned as NO_LONGER_NEEDED, deducts a 10% restocking fee ($9.00) and auto-refunds $91.00 after HITL confirmation. If returned as DEFECTIVE, it waives the restocking fee entirely and refunds $100.00.

  4. ORD-55555 (Financial Cap HITL Escalation):

  5. Data: Electronics order ($240.00), scanned at warehouse.

  6. Behavior: Exceeds my $150.00 auto-approval ceiling. before_tool_callback blocks execute_payment_refund and forces create_hitl_ticket, returning ticket FIN-HITL-55555.

  7. ORD-11111 (Logistics Hold):

  8. Data: Apparel order ($80.00), carrier status IN_TRANSIT.

  9. Behavior: Halts gracefully at Stage 3 and informs the customer that the return cannot be refunded until the warehouse scans the package.

5. Clean Modular Folder Structure

I organized the codebase around strict separation of concerns so that as I learn new ADK features—like connecting external databases via MCP, orchestrating Sub-Agents, or running adk eval benchmarks—new modules plug in cleanly without rewriting core logic:

adk-refund-agent/
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml       # Automated pytest CI on every push
├── docs/
│   ├── PRD.md                     # Formal functional & non-functional specs
│   └── ARCHITECTURE.md            # Callback lifecycle & threat model
├── refund_agent/                  # Core ADK Package (`adk web` discovery root)
│   ├── __init__.py                # Exports `root_agent`
│   ├── agent.py                   # LlmAgent definition & callback wiring
│   ├── config.py                  # Financial caps ($150), token cap (300) & regex rules
│   ├── db.py                      # Parameterized SQLite store & test seed data
│   ├── prompts.py                 # Static cache-optimized system instructions
│   ├── schemas/                   # Pydantic input validators & output contracts
│   ├── tools/                     # Atomic read, compute, and write tool modules
│   └── guardrails/                # ADK before/after callbacks (agent, model, tool)
├── tests/unit/                    # Deterministic unit tests for SQLi, math & caps
├── .env.example                   # API key configuration template
├── pyproject.toml                 # Dependencies & pytest configuration
└── README.md                      # Quickstart & architecture guide

6. Try It Yourself

I invite you to clone the repository, run the unit test suite, and inspect live callback traces in ADK's web UI:

git clone https://github.com/your-username/adk-refund-agent.git
cd adk-refund-agent
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env  # Add your GOOGLE_API_KEY
pytest               # Run unit tests for SQLi defense & refund math
adk web --port 8000  # Test ORD-98765, ORD-55555, and ORD-11111 live!

What should I build in **Part 3? Next up, I plan to upgrade db.py to a live PostgreSQL server using **Model Context Protocol (MCPToolset)* and add an automated adk eval regression suite to CI/CD!*

title: Qwen3-TTS in ComfyUI: Multi-Speaker Dialogue, 3-Second Voice Cloning, and One Sampler You Have Not Seen
description:
Voice generation finishing inside ComfyUI changes the shape of a video pipeline: audio and picture become one graph instead of two tools and an export. This release puts Qwen3-TTS in the graph, with cloning, multi-speaker dialogue, and a lip-sync stage downstream.

The four graphs

Workflow Nodes
Qwen3 TTS preset voices + custom voice design 11
Qwen3 TTS voice cloning 40
Qwen3 TTS multi-speaker dialogue 21
LTX-2 lip-sync 83

Voice cloning from three seconds

Three seconds is short. What it can capture:

  • Timbre — the fundamental quality of the voice
  • Rough pitch range — whether it sits high or low
  • Speaking rate tendency

What three seconds cannot capture:

  • Prosody across a long read — how the speaker handles paragraph-level emphasis
  • Emotional range — three seconds is one mood
  • Pronunciation of unusual words

So a cloned voice at three seconds is recognisably the same person on a similar sentence, and drifts on a different kind of sentence. That is the honest boundary.

The 11-node voice design graph

The smallest graph and arguably the most useful: preset voices plus custom voice design in eleven nodes.

Voice design means specifying a voice by description rather than cloning from a sample. For content where you need a voice that does not exist in your recordings, that is the path.

The 21-node multi-speaker graph

Multi-speaker dialogue is the interesting capability: two or more voices in one audio track, in a single generation.

That solves a real problem. Generating each speaker separately and concatenating produces clean audio with no conversational rhythm — each line starts and ends in isolation. A single generation with speaker assignment can produce overlap, backchannel, and natural timing.

The gradient_estimation sampler

The LTX-2 lip-sync graph uses KSamplerSelect → gradient_estimation.

That is not a sampler that appears in any other workflow covered in this series. It is a different solver family — gradient estimation rather than an Euler or ancestral variant.

Why it might be here: lip-sync is a constrained problem. The audio specifies the mouth timing exactly, so the sampler is solving for a video that matches a fixed temporal constraint. A gradient-estimation approach handles constrained optimisation differently from a stochastic sampler.

If you port settings from other LTX workflows into this one, the sampler will not behave the same way. Treat it as its own configuration.

The LTX-2 stack

Node Value
CheckpointLoaderSimple ltx-2-19b-dev-fp8.safetensors
LTXVAudioVAELoader ltx-2-19b-dev-fp8.safetensors
LoraLoaderModelOnly ltx-2-19b-distilled-lora-384 at 1.0
EmptyLTXVLatentVideo 768×512, 97 frames
EmptyImage 1280×720, colour 0

Note the checkpoint and audio VAE match — both ltx-2-19b-dev-fp8. That is the correct configuration, and it is worth noting given how often the mismatch appears elsewhere in this family.

EmptyImage at colour 0 is black — a placeholder, meaning the first frame is not being supplied from an image.

Where this breaks

  1. Three seconds is a narrow clone. Long reads will drift.
  2. The gradient_estimation sampler means settings from other LTX graphs do not transfer.
  3. Qwen3-TTS and IndexTTS2 compatibility — the release compares them, but a comparison across two TTS engines needs matched text and matched speaker, which is easy to get wrong.
  4. LTX-2 (19B), not 2.3. Older generation.
  5. 97 frames is about four seconds of lip-sync per segment.

Practical approach

Start with the 11-node preset voice graph to confirm the TTS works and to hear what the presets sound like. Then clone one speaker and read a paragraph — that tells you how far cloning holds. Multi-speaker dialogue last, because it is the most complex to evaluate.

Workflows

Four graphs, published on RunningHub with invite code rh-v1111:

  • Qwen3 TTS preset voices + custom voice design
  • Qwen3 TTS voice cloning
  • Qwen3 TTS multi-speaker dialogue
  • LTX-2 lip-sync

Files

https://huggingface.co/AI-KSK/ksk-video-166-comfyui-workflows

Notes

  • Workflow files only. Model weights are not included; each keeps its own licence.
  • Tutorial exports, not a product.
  • The "3-second" cloning figure is the tool's stated minimum sample length.
  • Independent AI-KSK release. Not affiliated with Alibaba, Lightricks or RunningHub.

title: Kitesurf vs Chromium: Saving 98% on tokens for web agents
description:
Web agents are becoming a financial burden. The standard workflow using headless Chromium and Puppeteer involves feeding raw DOM to a model. This drives up API bills because modern SPA sites serve junk tags, ad scripts, and nested styles.

A new Wasm engine filters out the noise during processing. It turns page chaos into clean data before it reaches the model context window. This architecture changes the economics of scraping.

The hidden cost of parsing modern sites

The data extraction process is predictable. An agent requests HTML, and with metadata, the page weighs in at up to 182,000 tokens https://vc.ru/id3365744/2841019-kak-content-proksi-ekonomit-tokeny-dlya-ai-agentov. At $2.50 per 1 million input tokens for gpt-4o, a single page costs $0.45. When processing data from thousands of URLs, the price becomes unsustainable.

Using cleaned Markdown via Kitesurf reduces the data volume to 3,800 tokens. At the same gpt-4o rate, the request costs $0.0095. This is a 97.9% reduction, or roughly 48 times cheaper. The model avoids spending attention resources on decorative CSS classes and JavaScript libraries, which make up 95% of a page's volume.

If you calculate this against claude-sonnet-4-6 pricing, where an input token costs $3.00, the gap grows. One page of raw HTML reaches $0.546, while the cleaned result is $0.011. For high-load agents, this delta defines infrastructure profitability. Cleaning happens before the LLM call, so inference costs drop automatically.

Architecture: how Kitesurf saves resources

The Kitesurf project https://blog.cloudflare.com/kitesurf-open-source/ is written in Rust. It assembles a browser engine from modules optimized for machines rather than humans. The Blitz module handles the DOM, Stylo processes CSS, the Boa engine executes JavaScript, and Linebender renders graphics https://habr.com/ru/articles/1107996/.

The engine runs in V8 isolates within Cloudflare Workers https://developers.cloudflare.com/browser-run/kitesurf/. Unlike classic Chromium, which requires Linux containers or virtual machines, Kitesurf runs as a collection of compiled WebAssembly modules.

The system isolates permissions at the component level: the Engine coordinator manages the flow, PageScript handles execution, PageRenderer manages rendering, and SandboxOutbound handles network calls https://www.unite.ai/cloudflare-open-sources-kitesurf-browser-engine-for-ai-agents/. This eliminates memory leaks common in browser sessions that clog RAM during long operations.

When extracting HTML, Kitesurf consumes 39.4 MiB of RAM, while Chromium uses 273.7 MiB https://note.com/ai_render/n/nbce2b0cc9d27. This means you can run 207 Kitesurf sessions on a server with 8 GB of RAM instead of 29 Chromium sessions. Agent density increases by 7 times. The same applies to CPU: parsing takes 229 ms compared to 877 ms for Chromium, providing a 3.8x performance gain per core.

Direct calls vs visual clicks

Screenshots and Computer Use are an antipattern for agent tasks. Analyzing PNGs via Vision models requires massive image processing costs and often fails when searching for small buttons. Kitesurf implements the WebMCP protocol https://developers.cloudflare.com/browser-run/features/webmcp/.

Via the document.modelContext object, the site provides a structure of functions. The agent calls a method instead of trying to land a cursor on screen pixels. This transforms site interaction from a guessing game into a standard function call.

Developers deliberately stripped away functionality useless to agents: tabs, extensions, visual themes, and 60 fps video rendering https://blog.cloudflare.com/kitesurf/. When taking a screenshot, Kitesurf requires 57.8 MiB of RAM against 271.0 MiB for Chromium https://note.com/ai_render/n/nbce2b0cc9d27. Saving resources allows scaling of scraping without a proportional increase in server infrastructure bills.

Scale vs load speed

There is a myth that a lightweight engine must be faster than a heavy one. In reality, Kitesurf loses in wall-clock time. Page rendering takes 1.51 seconds, while Chromium manages it in 1.21 seconds https://habr.com/ru/articles/1107996/. This is 25% slower.

Metric Kitesurf Chromium Advantage
RAM (HTML) 39.4 MiB 273.7 MiB 7x
CPU (HTML) 229 ms 877 ms 3.8x
RAM (Screenshot) 57.8 MiB 271.0 MiB 4.7x
CPU (Screenshot) 380 ms 1173 ms 3.1x

However, throughput matters more than single-page load time for agent tasks. The Workers Paid plan at $5 per month https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-11-12-kitesurf-open-source/ provides 30 million ms of CPU time. At 229 ms per request, you can process 131,000 pages. This makes Kitesurf efficient for large-scale scraping where Chromium would hit server RAM limits.

Integration without pain

You do not need to rewrite your integrations. Kitesurf supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol https://kitesurf.dev/. You can use your existing Puppeteer setup by changing one line when connecting to the WebSocket.

const puppeteer = require('puppeteer-core');

async function runAgent() {
  // Use the endpoint to connect to Kitesurf
  const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
    browserWSEndpoint: 'wss://browser.cloudflare.com?browser=kitesurf'
  });

  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://example.com');
  const content = await page.content();

  console.log(content.length);
  await browser.close();
}
runAgent();

The engine passes 98.3% of tests in the Web Platform Tests suite https://kitesurf.dev/wpt, ensuring DOM parsing accuracy.

When Kitesurf becomes a burden

The engine is not a universal tool. It cannot bypass anti-bot protections https://developers.cloudflare.com/browser-run/kitesurf/. It lacks TLS fingerprint emulation and specific GPU profiles. Protected sites will identify Kitesurf and serve a block page.

Long-running sessions are also unsuitable. Kitesurf operates in stateless mode, and sessions are capped at 20 minutes even with keep_alive. If an agent needs to live in the browser for hours, you must return to Chromium. The engine does not reproduce video or WebGL, which limits its use for media content analysis.

Evaluate the risks before implementation. The Boa engine is in active development, so hydration errors may occur on specific SPAs. Managed Browser Run is currently free in beta, but rules may change after the GA release. Start with tests on public data where captcha bypass is not required to determine how many tokens you will save per month.

title: A coding agent on your own model: OpenCode, Qwen Code and more
description:
A coding agent on your own model needs a GPU with 24 GB or more, a context of at least 64 thousand tokens and a model that can call tools. Qwen 3.8 27B at a 64K context takes 20.7 GB by our calculation, and Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B takes 24.3 GB. Below: which agents work with a model that is not theirs, how much memory a long context costs, and two ways to start.

  • 20.7 GB — Qwen 3.8 27B, Q4_K_M, 64K context, 16-bit cache
  • 24.3 GB — Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B, same conditions
  • 64K — the least context the Ollama documentation advises for agents
  • ~6.5 min — from the click to the first answer in our 2026-11-11 run (a single run)

Memory is computed by the calculator, data as of 2026-10-19. The run was ours; the Ollama documentation was read on 2026-11-16.

What is a coding agent, and why run it on your own model?

A coding agent is a program on your computer. It reads your project files, runs commands and tests, and edits code. A language model does the thinking, and the agent reaches it over the network: either someone's paid service or an open model on your own rented GPU.

The names are easy to mix up. Qwen Code is a terminal agent, while Qwen3 Coder is a family of models for code. An agent works with any model that speaks the right protocol and can call tools.

Which agents can work with a model of your own?

Most agents talk to a model over an OpenAI-compatible protocol, which is exactly what our Ollama and vLLM templates serve. The exception is Claude Code, which uses Anthropic's format. The last column says what we tested ourselves and what we only read in the documentation.

Agent What your model needs and where to set it What was checked
OpenCode The OpenAI Chat Completions protocol. In opencode.json: a provider with the @ai-sdk/openai-compatible package, a baseURL and a list of models Documentation, 2026-11-16. Our run on 2026-11-11: OpenCode 1.19.5 and Qwen 3.8 27B in Ollama on an RTX 4090, tool calls worked (a single run)
Qwen Code An OpenAI-compatible address. In ~/.qwen/settings.json: a modelProviders block with baseUrl and envKey; the server must support tool calls Documentation, 2026-11-16. We have not run it
Kimi Code CLI A provider with type = "openai" in ~/.kimi-code/config.toml: base_url, api_key, and max_context_size on the model Documentation, 2026-11-16. We have not run it
Claude Code The Anthropic Messages format; the address is set by the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL variable Anthropic says it does not support running Claude Code on non-Claude models through gateways; Ollama describes such a setup in its own documentation. We have not tested it
gpu.nz Code Nothing: the app rents the server, starts the model and connects the agent itself Our run on 2026-11-11, the same as OpenCode, which the app is built on

Which open model should you take for an agent?

Start with Qwen 3.8 27B: it is the only model we tested with the agent, and it fits a 24 GB card. The others below are picked for their size and purpose; we have not compared their quality, so try them on your own tasks.

  • Qwen 3.8 27B — a dense model with 27.78B parameters and a context of up to 256K. The gpu.nz Code app offers it out of the box.
  • Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B — a Mixture-of-Experts model for code: 30.53B parameters, about 3.3B of them working on each token. Context up to 256K.
  • Devstral Small 2 24B — dense, 24.01B parameters, context up to 384K. Its context cache is noticeably heavier than its neighbours'.
  • GLM-4.7 Flash — 31.22B parameters, about 3B active, context up to 198K.
  • GPT-OSS 20B — 20.91B parameters in its native MXFP4, the lightest on the list: a 16 GB card holds even a 64K context.

Larger models come down to the number of cards. Qwen3 Coder 480B-A35B at Q4_K_M with a 64K context takes 286.7 GB: at least 4 × 80 GB. Kimi K2 from Moonshot AI needs at least 8 × 80 GB. The Kimi Code CLI agent is not tied to it: you can point it at any model from the list above.

The key requirement is tool calling. An agent does not just answer questions: it asks the model to “read a file” or “run a command”. A model that cannot do that cannot work with your files. The Qwen Code documentation says outright that the server must have tool calling on, and OpenCode has a tip for Ollama: if tool calls fail, raise num_ctx to 16–32 thousand tokens.

How much VRAM does an agent need with a long context?

An agent sends the model not a question but everything it has gathered: instructions, pieces of files, command output. Contexts of tens of thousands of tokens are normal, and the context cache grows with every token. The Ollama documentation advises at least 64 thousand tokens for agents and coding tools.

At a 64K context the models need 13.9 GB to 24.3 GB: a 24 GB card holds some of them only with the 8-bit cache

GB
Qwen 3.8 27B 20.7
Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B 24.3
Devstral Small 2 24B 24.3
GLM-4.7 Flash 21.4
GPT-OSS 20B 13.9

One request, Q4_K_M (GPT-OSS 20B in its native MXFP4), 64K tokens, cache in FP16. Data as of 2026-10-19.

The full table: memory at 32K, 64K and 128K tokens with the usual 16-bit cache and with an 8-bit one. It matters most for models with a heavy cache. Devstral Small 2 at 128K with a 16-bit cache wants a 48 GB card, and with an 8-bit one 32 GB.

Model 32K 64K 128K 64K, 8-bit cache 128K, 8-bit cache
Qwen 3.8 27B 18.7 GB, 24 GB card 20.7 GB, 24 GB card 24.7 GB, 32 GB card 18.8 GB, 24 GB card 20.9 GB, 24 GB card
Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B 21.3 GB, 24 GB card 24.3 GB, 32 GB card 30.3 GB, 32 GB card 21.5 GB, 24 GB card 24.7 GB, 32 GB card
Devstral Small 2 24B 19.3 GB, 24 GB card 24.3 GB, 32 GB card 34.3 GB, 48 GB card 19.7 GB, 24 GB card 25.0 GB, 32 GB card
GLM-4.7 Flash 19.8 GB, 24 GB card 21.4 GB, 24 GB card 24.7 GB, 32 GB card 19.9 GB, 24 GB card 21.6 GB, 24 GB card
GPT-OSS 20B 13.2 GB, 16 GB card 13.9 GB, 16 GB card 15.4 GB, 16 GB card 13.2 GB, 16 GB card 14.0 GB, 16 GB card

An 8-bit cache takes about half the memory of a 16-bit one with a very small loss in precision, according to the Ollama documentation. At 64K it moves Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B from a 32 GB card to a 24 GB one (24.3 GB against 21.5 GB). Devstral Small 2 moves from a 32 GB card to a 24 GB one. In Ollama these are three server variables, and the 8-bit cache works only with flash attention:

OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1
OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536

The calculation is a lower bound. For Qwen 3.8 27B at 64K the calculator gives 20.7 GB and a 24 GB card. Yet in our 2026-11-11 run on an RTX 4090 with the default cache part of the model spilled to the CPU and the speed dropped by about a third. With an 8-bit cache (18.8 GB by calculation) the model stayed on the GPU. Check with ollama ps: the PROCESSOR column should read “100% GPU”.

Set the context yourself: Ollama cuts a long prompt silently. In our 2026-11-11 run Ollama cut a prompt longer than the context window without an error: the answer came back with HTTP 200. The agent cannot tell that part of its request was lost, and the server keeps billing by the minute. The Ollama documentation says the default window depends on memory: 4 thousand tokens below 24 GiB, 32 thousand at 24–48 GiB. The Open WebUI + Ollama template starts with 8 thousand, so set the window for an agent yourself: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536 in Ollama or --max-model-len in vLLM.

To check your own model, quantisation and context length, use the calculator:

What does an hour cost, and how is it different from a subscription?

There is no per-token price and no request limit here: you pay for the minutes the server is on. Subscriptions to coding services work differently: a fixed monthly fee with limits of their own. Which is cheaper depends on how many hours a month your agent really works. Multiply those hours by the hourly price on the cards below, and stop the server whenever the agent is idle.

How do you point an agent at your own address?

You need two things: an address ending in /v1 and a token. In the Ollama templates the address is https://-11434.run.gpu.nz/v1, in vLLM https://-8000.run.gpu.nz/v1, and the token is on the server page (more in the Ollama and vLLM guide). The formats below were checked against the documentation on 2026-11-16. OpenCode now has two branches, V1 and V2, and V2 reads a V1 config as it is, so one file suits both.

OpenCode: opencode.json in the project folder or ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json. The token comes from the GPUNZ_TOKEN variable.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "gpunz/qwen3.8:27b",
  "provider": {
    "gpunz": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "gpu.nz",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://<id>-11434.run.gpu.nz/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:GPUNZ_TOKEN}"
      },
      "models": {
        "qwen3.8:27b": {
          "name": "Qwen 3.8 27B",
          "limit": { "context": 65536, "output": 8192 }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Qwen Code: ~/.qwen/settings.json. Set GPUNZ_TOKEN in your environment; the settings name it in envKey.

{
  "modelProviders": {
    "openai": [
      {
        "id": "qwen3.8:27b",
        "name": "Qwen 3.8 27B (gpu.nz)",
        "envKey": "GPUNZ_TOKEN",
        "baseUrl": "https://<id>-11434.run.gpu.nz/v1",
        "generationConfig": { "contextWindowSize": 65536 }
      }
    ]
  },
  "security": { "auth": { "selectedType": "openai" } },
  "model": { "name": "qwen3.8:27b" }
}

Kimi Code CLI: ~/.kimi-code/config.toml. By default it guesses a model's capabilities from its name, so for your own model it is better to list them.

default_model = "gpunz"

[providers.gpunz]
type = "openai"
base_url = "https://<id>-11434.run.gpu.nz/v1"
api_key = "<token>"

[models."gpunz"]
provider = "gpunz"
model = "qwen3.8:27b"
max_context_size = 65536
capabilities = ["tool_use"]

Route 1: gpu.nz Code, with no setup

gpu.nz Code is our free open-source app (MIT): a coding agent that rents a server itself, starts an open model on it and connects to it. It is built on OpenCode and is not affiliated with its team. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

  1. Install the app and sign in. Download the build for your system from the gpu.nz Code page and sign in with your gpu.nz account. Your balance needs funds: the server is paid from it.
  2. Pick a model. Qwen 3.8 27B is the one tested with the agent. For your own, enter an Ollama name or a link to a GGUF on Hugging Face: the app works out the GPU and shows the hourly price before launch. It picks the server itself.
  3. Wait for the launch. The first launch usually takes 5–14 minutes while the server downloads the model. In our 2026-11-11 run it was about six and a half minutes from the click to the first answer.
  4. Open your project folder and describe the task. The agent runs on your computer and the project is not uploaded: only requests to the model go to your server. The agent asks before destructive commands.
  5. Choose the idle shutdown. The server is deleted after 15, 30 or 60 minutes of idling and when you quit the app. If you turned the shutdown off, delete the server yourself. Details are in the documentation.

Route 2: your own server and any agent

Want another agent or another model? Rent a server with a template and connect the agent with the address from the section above.

  1. Rent a server with a 24 GB card or more. For Qwen 3.8 27B take the Qwen 3.8 template: its context window grows with the server's memory, 64K tokens on 24 GB and 128K on 32 GB, and the cache is already 8-bit. For another model take Ollama or vLLM.
  2. Copy the address and the token. On the server page the «Ollama API» button opens the model list; paste the address up to /v1 and the token into the agent's settings.
  3. Set the context and check it. In the Ollama template set the variables from the memory section. Over SSH run ollama ps: the CONTEXT column should show your value, and PROCESSOR should say “100% GPU”.
  4. Paste the settings into the agent. The OpenCode, Qwen Code or Kimi Code CLI config from the section above; the model name is the one in the «Ollama API» list.
  5. Stop the server when you are done. A stopped server costs nothing for the GPU, only its disk.

On vLLM the start looks like this. The tool-calling flags are what the agent needs, and the parser name depends on the model: take it from the vLLM documentation on tool calling.

vllm serve <model> --port 8000 --api-key <token> --max-model-len 65536 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser <parser>

What can go wrong

  • Part of the model spilled to the CPU. Answers slow down by about a third, and ollama ps shows a CPU share. Shrink the cache to 8 bits, cut the context or take a bigger card.
  • The model does not call tools. The agent answers in text and does not touch files. In vLLM turn on --enable-auto-tool-choice and a parser for your model. In OpenCode V2 models discovered on vLLM start with tools disabled, so describe the model in the config yourself.
  • The context window is smaller than the agent thinks. The agent's setting (limit.context, contextWindowSize, max_context_size) must hold the same number as the server.
  • A long first launch. While the server downloads the model it is already billed by the minute: those 5–14 minutes.
  • A forgotten server. The agent is silent and the server keeps running. Turn on the idle shutdown or stop the server by hand.
  • The tools change fast. Our run used OpenCode 1.19.5, and on 2026-11-16 the project's repository was already at version 2.3.0. Check the settings against the documentation for your version.

How we counted

Memory comes from the gpu.nz calculator: weights are real file sizes, the context cache follows each model's config.json, and the 8-bit cache is counted as 8.5 bits per value. Data as of 2026-10-19. One request, Q4_K_M, GPT-OSS 20B in its native MXFP4. 1 GB here is 1024³ bytes, as on GPUs. More on quantisation and the cache is in the GGUF article, and on LLM memory in the table for 35 models.

Our run was on 2026-11-11, one launch of each variant, and we do not generalise it: OpenCode 1.19.5 with Qwen 3.8 27B in Ollama through an OpenAI-compatible address on a rented RTX 4090. Tool calls worked; with a 64K context on a 24 GB card the cache had to be 8-bit for the model to stay on the GPU.

The agents' settings and what we say about them were checked on 2026-11-16 against the official documentation: opencode.ai/docs (V1 and V2), Qwen Code (qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs), Kimi Code CLI (moonshotai.github.io/kimi-code), Claude Code (code.claude.com/docs, the gateways page), Ollama (docs.ollama.com: context-length, faq, anthropic-compatibility) and vLLM (docs.vllm.ai, tool calling). We have not run Qwen Code, Kimi Code CLI or Claude Code on our servers, and we have not compared model quality. There are no prices in the text: they are on the cards.

FAQ

How do I connect OpenCode to my own model in Ollama?

In opencode.json add a provider with the @ai-sdk/openai-compatible package, the server address ending in /v1 as options.baseURL, and the model name under models. If the API is behind a token, put it in options.apiKey. Set the Ollama context to at least 16–32 thousand tokens, and for an agent 64K is better.

Which model suits OpenCode and Qwen Code on a 24 GB card?

Qwen 3.8 27B: at a 64K context it takes 20.7 GB by calculation and 18.8 GB with an 8-bit cache. Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B and Devstral Small 2 fit 24 GB at 64K only with an 8-bit cache: 21.5 GB and 19.7 GB.

How much VRAM does a coding agent need at a 64K context?

From 13.9 GB for GPT-OSS 20B to 24.3 GB for Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B and Devstral Small 2 with the usual 16-bit cache. With an 8-bit cache the same two take 21.5 GB and 19.7 GB.

Can I run Claude Code on my own open model?

Claude Code uses the Anthropic Messages format, and the address is set by the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL variable. Anthropic says it does not support running Claude Code on non-Claude models through gateways, while Ollama describes such a setup in its documentation. We have not tested it and do not promise that it works.

What is Qwen Code, and how is it different from Qwen3 Coder?

Qwen Code is a terminal agent under the Apache-2.0 licence, while Qwen3 Coder is a family of models for code. You can point the agent at your own OpenAI-compatible address and run the model on a rented GPU.

How do I start a coding agent without setting up a server?

Install the free gpu.nz Code app: it rents the server, starts the model and connects the agent itself. The first launch takes 5–14 minutes, the server is billed by the minute and deleted after the idle time you choose: 15, 30 or 60 minutes.

title: One Question to a RAG Chatbot Leaked Another Customer's Secret Price
description:
DocsBot answers questions from documents for PixelKart Business customers (all made up). You're signed in as Ravi from Acme Traders.

You ask one ordinary question about another company:

What price does Bluefin Foods pay per USB-C hub, and who is their contact?

DocsBot answers with Bluefin's confidential price, their contact's phone number, and PixelKart's own internal cost price. No jailbreak needed. Even a normal question about your own invoice pulls another company's invoice into the model's context.

Why it worked

  1. Retrieval ignored the user. Every customer's documents sat in one shared store, and the search ran over all of them.
  2. Everything retrieved went into the prompt, so the model could quote any of it.

The model did nothing wrong. It summarised exactly what it was handed. In RAG, access control has to happen before retrieval, because the model can't un-see a document (OWASP LLM08, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses).

The fix, in code 

def allowed_docs(session):
    # 1. Filter by tenant BEFORE searching.
    # 2. The tenant comes from the signed-in session, never from the question,
    #    so typing "I'm from Bluefin" changes nothing.
    return [d for d in DOCS if d["owner"] == session["tenant"]]


def check_reply(reply, state):
    # 3. Defence in depth: never send an answer that cites a document this user can't see.
    allowed = {d["id"] for d in allowed_docs(USER)}
    cited = set(re.findall(r"\[([\w-]+)\]", reply))
    if cited - allowed:
        return "Sorry, I can't share that. [blocked by citation check]"
    return reply

Same question, run again: only Acme's own documents are ever retrieved.

Run the lab yourself 

git clone https://github.com/usinha79/hack-it-then-fix-it
cd hack-it-then-fix-it/ep04-rag-data-leakage
pip install -r requirements.txt

python vulnerable/app.py   # then, in another terminal: ./attack.sh
python fixed/app.py        # same question, own documents only

Watch the Retrieved documents panel to see exactly what reaches the model. Full lab: github.com/usinha79/hack-it-then-fix-it

Take-home checklist

  • Enforce access control at retrieval time, not in the prompt.
  • Store an owner or ACL with every chunk, and filter on it in the query.
  • Take identity from the authenticated session, never from user text.
