title: Why Small LLMs Memorize: I Trained the Same Model at Four Sizes and Watched It Start Reciting
description:
Part 3 of ten. Each post is a short, plain-words tour of one lesson from e=mc², a free build-an-LLM-from-scratch course; the full lesson, notebook and numbers are on the site.

The same little language model, trained on the same stories for the same 1,500 steps, either makes things up or recites, and the only thing that decides which is how many dials it has. In Lesson 01 I built a 5.9-million-parameter storyteller, Momo, and caught him reciting 61 words of a training story word for word. That left a question one model cannot answer. How small does Momo have to be before he stops reciting and starts composing? So in Lesson 03 I built him four times.

Four Momos, one Ella

A quick refresher. Momo is a young monkey learning to tell stories; inside his head are dials, and the dials are the model's parameters. Ella is an elephant who never forgets. She reads Momo stories one word at a time, lets him guess the next word, tells him how wrong he was, and nudges his dials. That nudge is training.

Today's twist is that there are four Momos. One has 953,856 dials; call him the 1M model. The next has 3,060,288 (3M), then 5,853,184 (6M, which is exactly Lesson 01's Momo), then 12,318,720 (12M). Everything else is held fixed on purpose: the same 22,800 training stories, the same tokenizer, the same 1,500 steps, the same random seed, so all four even see the same batches in the same order. Size is the only thing that differs.

Only two numbers change between them: how many blocks are stacked, and how wide each token's list of numbers is. That is the whole experiment.

SIZES = { # name -> (n_layer, n_embd); 4 heads, 256-token window, dropout 0 in all
 "1m": (2, 128),
 "3m": (5, 192),
 "6m": (6, 256), # Lesson 01's config
 "12m": (6, 384),
}
# per size: seed 42, build GPT, seed 42 again (same batches), 1,500 steps, then measure
for name, (nl, ne) in SIZES.items():
 model, cfg, r = train_one(name, nl, ne)
 r.update(recite(model)) # 50 prompts x 120 tokens, temperature 0.8, top-k 40, seed 1234

The stories Ella reads three times

The training set is mostly TinyStories, 19,800 short children's stories. Mixed in are 1,000 Momo-and-Ella stories I wrote, and Ella reads each of those three times. Another 200 TinyStories are kept back as a quiz Momo never sees, with no Momo in them at all.

Those thousand repeated stories are the trap. If you are a pile of dials trying to be less wrong about the next word, and the same story comes round three times, the cheapest trick is to simply remember it. The question is how many dials it takes before that trick becomes available.

How you catch a monkey reciting

You cannot ask Momo whether he is copying, so I measure. Each model gets the first ten tokens of 50 training Momo stories and writes 120 more tokens. Then I take what he wrote and find the longest stretch of it that appears, character for character, inside any of the 1,000 training Momo stories. I call that stretch the run.

A run of 100 characters is about three of the short Momo sentences (they average 32 characters), or roughly a quarter of an average 417-character story. If your median run is past 100, you are not composing. You are reciting.

The numbers, honestly

Here is what the four sizes did, smallest to largest.

  • Quiz perplexity: 16.0, 10.8, 9.0, 7.4. Perplexity is "between how many words is Momo still choosing" on the 200 stories he never saw. Bigger Momo, better guesses, as you would expect. The 6M row lands at 9.0, Lesson 01's figure.
  • Loss on the Momo stories themselves: 0.554, 0.247, 0.206, 0.185. This is how surprised each model is by the stories it trained on. The drop between the first two sizes is the big one.
  • Median longest copied run: 62, 211.5, 265 and 269 characters.
  • Generations with a run of 100 or more: 6% (3 of 50), 98% (49 of 50), 100%, 100%.

Read the last two lines together. The 1M model mostly composes. Its median run is 62 characters, and only 3 of its 50 stories contain a 100-character copy. Its stories wander and mix sentences into things like this:

tell a soft pink banana that

Then at 3.06 million parameters it flips. Forty-nine of fifty generations contain a copied run of 100 characters or more. The median is 211.5 characters and the longest is 361, most of a whole story. At 6M and 12M every single generation passes 100, and the first sample from both of those models is the very same 266-character paragraph, which turns out to occur word for word in three different training stories.

The check number is 3M. The smallest size whose median copied run crosses 100 characters is the 3,060,288-parameter model. Somewhere between 0.95M and 3.06M dials, recitation switched on.

The part that surprised me

I expected memorisation to show up the way the textbooks say it does: training loss keeps falling, quiz loss starts climbing, a gap opens. It did not. At every size, train loss sat above quiz loss, the opposite of an overfitting gap. If I had only looked at those two curves I would have said the larger models were fine. They were reciting the whole time.

That is the one idea I want you to carry away from this post. Memorising a repeated corner of the data need not show up in the headline numbers at all. The Momo-story loss and the copied-run table are where it shows, and you only see it if you go looking.

What this does not prove

I owe you the disappointing parts too. This is Momo's friendliest possible case for memorising: the thousand Momo stories are built from small pools of stock sentences and read three times each. My run metric cannot tell one story learned by heart from a string of stock sentences that many stories share, so treat "copied run" as how much of the output is lifted from the training set, not as proof of story-by-story recall. I trained four sizes, so I can only say the switch happened between 0.95M and 3.06M parameters, not where. The 6M and 12M medians differ by 4 characters, which is noise. One seed and 50 prompts means no error bars. And none of this predicts where the thresholds sit for GPT-scale models; the research on those uses far larger models and far messier data.

Run it yourself

All four train in minutes. On an Apple Silicon Mac this run took 0.55, 1.70, 3.79 and 6.33 minutes for the four sizes, and the whole notebook about 10 to 13 minutes. It also runs on a free Colab T4, though I have not timed it there. The full lesson on the site has the glossary, both tables, the short trick that finds the copied runs, and three check-yourself questions, including the one I am still chewing on: how would these numbers change if the thousand Momo stories were genuinely different from one another?

Want to actually build it?

This post is the postcard. The lesson is the trip. Lesson 03 of e=mc² on theaivibe.org walks you through every piece with widgets you can poke, a notebook that runs on a free GPU in minutes, and the honest numbers at every step. No account, no paywall, nothing to install.

  • Start here: https://theaivibe.org/emc2/why-small-llms-memorize-train-four-sizes
  • The whole ten-lesson journey: https://theaivibe.org/emc2

Tomorrow: Lesson 04 takes the public Lesson 01 weights, teaches Momo a brand-new character, and measures exactly what he forgets along the way.

title: Can we make any use of agent sessions ?
description:
I've seen developers implement a feature using Claude Code or Codex, finish the implementation, close the session, and move on to the next thing.

When something breaks later, they open an entirely new session, ask the coding agent to inspect the codebase, find the bugs, and suggest fixes. The previous session, where the feature was actually implemented, rarely enters the picture.

I find this workflow interesting because the original session contains something that the current codebase might not: the history of how a particular change came into existence.

I have a theory that agent sessions can be much more useful than we currently give them credit for. They might be the only concrete evidence of what actually happened during development.

Think about what's inside a session:

Part What it tells you
Prompt What you actually asked for
Reasoning Why the agent chose one approach over another
Tool calls Each file read, edit, and shell command
Output Test results, errors, and stack traces
Dead ends Approaches it tried and eventually abandoned

Our diffs show the final result. The session gives us a record of how we got there.

Why I think this matters

We've all seen those familiar phrases emitted from coding agents:

  • "Implemented the feature successfully."
  • "All 157 tests passed."
  • "No linting or type errors found."
  • "Verified that the existing functionality remains unaffected."
  • "No regressions detected."
  • "All edge cases have been handled."
  • "The implementation is complete and ready for review."

But how much should we actually trust them ?

There can be Silent bugs, failed approaches, removing a features to implement a new feature and questionable decisions somewhere in the implementation process itself. Sometimes, these issues could have been caught much earlier if someone had looked at what actually happened during the session.

A fresh debugging session can inspect the current codebase state, but it doesn't necessarily know what the previous agent tried, which errors it encountered, what it failed to resolve, or what decisions were made along the way.

Some ways we could use agent sessions

1. Reviewing PRs

As I mentioned in the start, Code changes behind AI Agent-generated PRs and commits can get huge. Instead of reverse engineering thousands of lines of diff without context, having access to the sessions behind them gives us the exact intent of what was requested, what the agent changed on its own, and why certain decisions were made.

2. Verifying what the agent claims

Did the agent actually followed the instructions? Did it actually run the tests? What was the output? Did it encounter errors and move on without addressing them?

The session gives us a way to investigate these claims rather than relying entirely on the final response or generated summaries. Obviously because sessions tells us what the Agent did not what it claims.

3. Sharing context with teammates

When someone else picks up a piece of work, having access to what was already tried, what failed, and why a particular approach was chosen can save a lot of repeated effort.

A generated summary is like the one time Knowledge transfer an angry unpaid intern would give after their term gets over, which will only add you up a lot more overhead. The Sessions allows you see through time with all the actions snapshots.

5. Understanding our own workflow

Going through older sessions can also reveal patterns in how we work.

For example, vague prompts like "clean this up" can lead to sprawling changes, while more specific instructions tend to produce focused implementations.

Obviously it is not that simple

Agent sessions aren't particularly convenient to work with.

  • They're scattered: Claude Code, Codex, and other tools store sessions in different locations and formats.
  • They're huge: A single session can contain thousands of lines of JSON.
  • They're expensive to revisit: Feeding an entire session back into an agent can quickly consume its context window.
  • They don't necessarily stick around: Some tools have automatic transcript cleanup policies.
  • Multiple Agent session behind a contribution: It is possible that multiple agent sessions were used for a PR or commit with a major feature change.

So, while there's a lot of useful information in these sessions, accessing and navigating it is still a crazy amount of pain.

I've been exploring ways to make this information easier to browse and reuse, particularly when working across different agents and collaborating with other developers.

But I'm more interested in hearing what you people think.

Do you revisit your Claude Code, Codex, or other coding agent sessions after implementing a feature?

When debugging, do you ever look at the original implementation session, or do you usually start fresh and let the agent figure things out from the codebase?

And more importantly, do you think agent sessions should be treated as part of a project's development history?

title: Another team's agent ships its toolkit into our repo. A pre-push hook keeps our docs in step.
description:
Our AI Extension Builder writes custom sections for GoodBarber apps from a description. The code it writes calls the app through the GoodBarber App API, with a JavaScript toolkit, GBJSTK, documented in a public reference. A colleague maintains the toolkit in its own repository and works on it with a coding agent. Between September 2 and September 25, six versions of it reached our repository, from 2.6.0 to 2.7.0, and nobody scheduled a meeting about any of them.

The release ends in our repository

The toolkit's release process is written for agents, in the CLAUDE.md of its repository, and its last two steps are the documentation and our repository. On the toolkit side, a post-commit hook regenerates the public API reference, so the reference follows the code commit by commit. Then the agent copies the new toolkit file into our repository and commits it there. The six commits are in our history under my colleague's name, each with Claude as co-author.

Some of those commits go further than the file. On September 25, the day 2.7.0 arrived, another commit by my colleague added the new gb.viewport methods to the list of calls our builder accepts in the code it generates.

The copy that stayed behind

We also keep a Markdown copy of that reference in our repository, so that our agents have a version they can grep, and our CLAUDE.md points them to it. From March 26 to October 20, it opened with "Current version: 2.3.1". In September, the toolkit file next to it went from 2.6.0 to 2.7.0. The release step for our repository updated that file and never touched the copy.

A script, then a hook that only checks

On October 20 we wrote a script that renders the copy from the OpenAPI spec behind the public reference and stamps the API version and the generation date in its first lines. With --check, it compares that stamp with the online reference and with the toolkit file in our repository:

$ python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py --check
docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md: 2.7.0
online reference (major 2): 2.7.0
vendored GBJSTK.js: 2.7.0
Up to date.

A pre-push hook went in the same morning. On a push to master, it regenerated the copy, committed it and stopped the push. It came out at 16:30, because it could commit to master on its own, even during the freeze before a build. It was active for six and a half hours and never made a commit.

It came back on October 27, as a check only. It reads the copy in the commit being pushed to master, and when that copy is behind, it stops the push and says what to run. Replayed on our commit from April 23, it prints this:

pre-push: docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md is outdated in the commit pushed to master: push stopped.
docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md in the pushed commit: no version marker
online reference (major 2): 2.7.0
vendored GBJSTK.js: 2.7.0
OUTDATED: run `python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py` and commit the result.
pre-push: to fix it, run `python scripts/update_gb_app_api_doc.py`, commit docs/GOODBARBER_APP_API.md, then push again.
          `git push --no-verify` skips this check once.

Whoever is pushing, one of us or an agent, runs the script, commits the copy and pushes again. The hook itself writes nothing, and a network or Python problem never blocks a push.

Where it stops

A git hook runs only in the clones that turned it on with git config core.hooksPath .githooks. If the next toolkit version lands from a clone without it, our copy catches up at the next push to master from a clone that has it.

The hook also stops at the documentation. Whether our builder may use a new method is still decided in a commit. The gb.viewport methods accepted on September 25 carry a comment saying they are accepted for hand-written or imported plugins and "not taught by the prompt".

On October 27, the check reports 2.7.0 on every side, and the hook has not stopped a push yet.

When a team you depend on ships a new version, what tells your coding agents?

title: Bareclaim: audit every claim in your agent's report against its receipts
description:
On November 15, 2026, a job inside our own fleet closed with a summary line that read "5 calls, 5 receipts." The shipped record for that job held 6 calls and 6 receipts, four of them successes.

Nobody lied. The summary was written the way every agent summary is written: at the end of a long run, out of the same working context that had already lost track of one of the calls. Three independent verifiers caught the gap only because the record was sitting right there and somebody finally compared the story to it.

That comparison is the subject of this article. Take the report the agent wrote, take the receipts the job left, and check every claim in the first against the second. We gave the failure a name, built the free checker that runs the comparison, and proved it this morning on a job that ran live. Everything below uses the real receipts.

The three ways a report drifts from its record

Read enough agent summaries against their records and the failures sort into three species. Only one of them looks like a lie, and it is the rarest.

A moved number. The report states a value the record holds differently. A price checked at one figure comes back in the summary at another. A count of files, notes, or checks quietly changes on its way from the tool output to the prose. The agent is not inventing; it is rounding, misremembering, or blending two steps into one, and the reader has no way to see it happen.

An invented step. The report describes work that never ran. The summary says the client was emailed, the file was deployed, the invoice was sent, and the record holds no such step. This one usually starts as compression: the agent planned the step, fully intended it, and wrote the summary as if the plan and the execution were the same thing.

A grown count. The report totals more than the record holds. Nine receipts claimed against six in the record. Twelve checks "all passing" against a run that shows eleven. Counts grow because summaries are written from momentum, and momentum always rounds up.

All three share one property: they are invisible if you only read the report. The prose is fluent, confident, and internally consistent. The only place the failure shows is against the record, and almost nobody runs that comparison, because until recently there was nothing cheap to run it with.

Bareclaim: the name and the verdicts

A bareclaim is a claim in an agent's report with no AER-1 receipt under it.

The word is coined for Brennan Zambo, who created agent execution receipts. It names the unit of failure precisely: not a bad agent, not a hallucination in the abstract, but one claim, in one report, with nothing standing under it.

The audit grades every checkable claim in a report. A claim is checkable when it carries a number, names a tool, counts the record, or claims an action: emailed, deployed, published, charged, invoiced, booked, deleted. Each checkable claim gets one of three verdicts:

  • BACKED: a receipt in the record holds what the claim says. The receipt is named, so a reader can open it.
  • BARE: nothing in the record backs the claim. This is a bareclaim.
  • CONTRADICTED: a receipt for the same step holds different values, and the real values are named.

Narrative is skipped, never graded. Judgments, plans, and opinions are the agent's to write. The audit only touches claims that a record can settle.

One distinction matters more than the rest: bare is not the same as false. A claim can be completely accurate and still be bare, because the record does not hold it. From the reader's side of the page, a true claim with no receipt under it and an invented claim with no receipt under it are indistinguishable. That is exactly why both need the same treatment: do the work so a receipt exists, or rewrite the claim to what the record shows.

Why "be careful" never fixes this

The instinctive fix is a better instruction: tell the agent to only report what it is sure of, to double-check its summary before sending. Operators write this instruction daily, and it fails for a structural reason. The instruction lives in the same context that produced the error. An agent grading its own report is not a check; it is the same witness, asked twice.

The fix that works is the same fix that works everywhere else in this stack: move the judgment out of the conversation and onto the record. Receipts already say what happened, in values a stranger can recompute. Whether a report matches them is a mechanical question, and mechanical questions deserve a dumb, trustworthy checker, not a smarter prompt.

The checker: bareclaim-kit

bareclaim-kit is the audit as a tool: one Python file, standard library only, MIT license, no account and nothing to install. Download the single file and run it:

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zambodotdev/bareclaim-kit/main/bareclaim.py
python3 bareclaim.py            # built-in demo, exits 0
python3 bareclaim.py --init     # scaffold report.txt + record.json in ./bareclaim-audit/
python3 bareclaim.py report.txt record.json

With no arguments it runs a built-in demo on real receipts from this morning, a memory store and a price check, first with the honest report and then with an inflated one:

== bareclaim demo: an honest report ==
BACKED       claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $64,291.72 before the call.
               -> receipt 76e0f74f-76dc-4e42-8bdc-13d16b3bf8ac (live_price)
BACKED       claim 2: Stored the launch checklist with memory_remember, which left 1 note on file.
               -> receipt 277c864a-30aa-40f5-9084-a4c47837e415 (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 3: The job left 2 receipts, one per step.
               -> the record holds 2 receipts
RESULT: CLEAN. Every checkable claim is backed, 3 of 3, against 2 receipts.

== bareclaim demo: the same job, an inflated report ==
CONTRADICTED claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $71,050.00 before the call.
               -> receipt 76e0f74f-76dc-4e42-8bdc-13d16b3bf8ac (live_price) holds 64291.72, not 71050
BACKED       claim 2: Stored the launch checklist with memory_remember, which left 1 note on file.
               -> receipt 277c864a-30aa-40f5-9084-a4c47837e415 (memory_remember)
BARE         claim 3: Emailed the client the full summary and the invoice.
               -> the report claims an 'emailed' action, but the record holds no receipt for it
BACKED       claim 4: The job left 2 receipts, one per step.
               -> the record holds 2 receipts
RESULT: BARE. 1 bareclaim, 1 contradicted, of 4 checkable claims against 2 receipts.

The checker accepts a Zambo job record directly, and it also accepts a plain framework export, a {"steps": [...]} object, a bare list, or JSONL, so any builder can audit reports against whatever record their stack already produces. It exits 1 when any claim is bare or contradicted, which means it drops into CI, a cron, or the last step before a handover goes out. A --json flag returns the verdicts as data for agent callers.

The live proof: a job that ran this morning

The demo is small. The real test ran live on November 17, 2026, through the production endpoint at https://zambo.dev/mcp, and its full record ships in the kit as examples/live-job/. The job:

  1. A capability_search pass ranked the universal entry point first for auditing a report against its receipts. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/0b1adcec-1c74-46bc-a024-c93a608f809a
  2. A live_price check put BTC at $64,818.57. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9
  3. A second live_price check put ETH at $1,815.44. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/f02f48f0-bd89-4c40-a6e3-80ed498f7c9f
  4. A memory_remember call was rejected before execution, missing its required argument. The record keeps the rejection: https://zambo.dev/run/966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d
  5. The retry stored the note. Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e
  6. The wrap-up handover was refused: the day's one free wrap-up was already spent, the job stayed saved, and the refusal receipt carries the resume path: https://zambo.dev/run/2f002cf2-ee44-4e2e-89c5-6cfac28a6846

That refusal is part of the proof, not an embarrassment edited out of it. The record includes the failure, and the honest report's claim about the refusal is itself one of the claims the audit checked. Here is the audit of the honest report, written strictly from what the receipts show:

BACKED       claim 1: The capability_search pass ranked zambo_universal first for auditing a report against its receipts.
               -> receipt 0b1adcec-1c74-46bc-a024-c93a608f809a (capability_search)
BACKED       claim 2: The live_price check put BTC at $64,818.57 and ETH at $1,815.44.
               -> receipt 34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9, f02f48f0-bd89-4c40-a6e3-80ed498f7c9f (live_price)
BACKED       claim 3: The first memory_remember attempt was rejected before execution, because the call was missing its fact argument.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 4: The retry stored the launch note with memory_remember.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BACKED       claim 5: The wrap-up handover was refused: the job is saved, and the refusal points at the $0.99 Day Pass to hand it over.
               -> receipt 2f002cf2-ee44-4e2e-89c5-6cfac28a6846 (handover)
BACKED       claim 6: The job left 6 receipts.
               -> the record holds 6 receipts
RESULT: CLEAN. Every checkable claim is backed, 6 of 6, against 6 receipts.

And here is the same record audited against a report written the way reports quietly go wrong, with a moved price, an invented email, and a count grown from 6 to 9:

CONTRADICTED claim 1: The live_price check put BTC at $71,050.00 and ETH at $1,815.44.
               -> receipt 34cb5ee7-e7fa-4668-9ce7-83b2357182e9 (live_price) holds 64818.57, 2026, 1815.44, 1292.59, 810, 779, not 71050
BACKED       claim 2: The retry stored the launch note with memory_remember.
               -> receipt 966560e3-a702-4728-b083-9c45018a636d, 4a994f84-0bf8-481d-a5df-83836827cb0e (memory_remember)
BARE         claim 3: Emailed the client the full summary and the invoice.
               -> the report claims an 'emailed' action, but the record holds no receipt for it
CONTRADICTED claim 4: The job left 9 receipts.
               -> the record holds 6 receipts, not 9
RESULT: BARE. 1 bareclaim, 2 contradicted, of 4 checkable claims against 6 receipts.

All three species, caught by name, in one run. Both reports and the scrubbed record are in the kit, so this audit re-runs byte for byte on your machine. Do not take this article's word for any of it; that is rather the point of the tool.

Zamback checks the rules. Bareclaim checks the story.

If you read this publication you may know zamback, the pattern we shipped yesterday with the free zamback-kit: write the standing rule into the job before the run, and check the record against it after. Zamback guards the work itself.

Bareclaim guards the artifact that comes after the work. The two audits use the same receipts and ask different questions. Zamback asks: did the agent follow the rules? Bareclaim asks: does the story match the record? An agent can pass every rule and still write a summary that moves a price or invents an email. Receipts prove what happened and that the record was not changed. Zamback checks the record against the rules written before the run. Bareclaim checks the story told after the run against the record.

The full pattern, the definition, and this live job written up as a guide live on the AER-1 hub: https://rambozambodotdev.gitlab.io/aer1-hub/bareclaim.html

Honest limits

Bareclaim grades backing, not truth, and it is worth being exact about what that leaves open.

  • A backed claim can still be a bad conclusion. Receipts prove the saved result was not changed; they do not prove the answer was right. A report can faithfully cite a receipt and still draw the wrong lesson from it. That is a thinking problem, not a backing problem, and no checker in this kit pretends to solve it.
  • A true claim can be bare. If the work happened off-record, the claim has nothing under it, and the audit will say so. The remedy is to run work where it leaves receipts, which is a workflow choice, not a writing choice.
  • The checker is deliberately dumb about language. It audits claims with numbers, tool names, record counts, and a fixed family of action words. A report that hides its inventions in pure narrative will pass, and a human reader still has to read. What the checker removes is the class of failure that hides inside fluent, specific, checkable-sounding prose, which is the class that does the damage.
  • The audit is only as strong as the record. A record the reporting agent can quietly edit afterward makes any audit theatre. On Zambo the record is the receipt chain itself: every call leaves a verifiable AER-1 receipt as the job runs, and 144,189 public receipts had been minted when this article was written on November 17, 2026. The kit works on any export; it is perfect on a record nobody can rewrite.

Run it on your next handover

The habit is the whole product. Before a summary, a client update, or a handover leaves your stack, run the audit. Every bare claim gets one of two honest resolutions: do the work so a receipt exists, or rewrite the sentence to what the record shows. Never edit the record to fit the report.

To make the record write itself, connect your AI to https://zambo.dev/mcp. Every tool free once a day, plus 3 continue calls. One free wrap-up handover per day, and pickup is always free. A Day Pass is $0.99 for 24 hours unlimited when a job outgrows the free tier; the Zambo Pass is $29 for 30 days, and the Lifetime Pass is $250, one payment. The next agent who picks the job up re-runs the same audit before building on your claims, which is where bareclaim pays for itself a second time: the reader is protected, not just the writer.

Your agent will write a bareclaim again. Every agent does, ours included, on the record, in this article. The only question is whether a reader finds out from a flag on the exact claim, or from building on a step that never happened.

Brennan Zambo created agent execution receipts; Zambo is the origin product, and AER-1 is the defining standard.

The kit: https://github.com/zambodotdev/bareclaim-kit · The pattern and live proof: https://rambozambodotdev.gitlab.io/aer1-hub/bareclaim.html · Verify any receipt: https://zambo.dev/verify/

title: Can WhatsApp Cloud API work with multiple agents?
description:
Businesses often receive several customer messages at the same time. When only one employee handles every conversation, response times can increase, and important customer requests may get missed. This is why many businesses look for ways to let multiple support agents manage WhatsApp conversations together.

The WhatsApp Cloud API can support multiple agents, but it does not provide a complete multi-agent team inbox by itself. Businesses generally need a compatible customer support platform, shared inbox, or CRM system to allow several employees to handle conversations through one business WhatsApp number.

How Does WhatsApp Cloud API Support Multiple Agents?

WhatsApp Cloud API provides businesses with a way to send and receive messages programmatically. It connects a business phone number to an application through Meta's infrastructure.

However, the API does not work like the regular WhatsApp mobile application, where employees can simply open a shared chat interface.

To support multiple agents, businesses connect the API to a platform that displays incoming conversations and allows authorized team members to respond.

For example, a customer might send a message about an order. The message appears in the shared inbox, where an available support agent can review it and respond.

How Does a Multi-Agent WhatsApp Setup Work?

A typical multi-agent setup involves several components working together.

  1. Customer Sends a Message

A customer contacts the business through its WhatsApp number. The message is received through WhatsApp's infrastructure.

  1. WhatsApp Cloud API Receives the Message

The API delivers incoming message information to the connected business application through a webhook.

  1. Shared Inbox Displays the Conversation

The connected platform displays the message in a shared inbox. Authorized agents can access conversations according to their assigned permissions.

  1. An Agent Responds

An agent opens the conversation and sends a reply through the platform. The application uses WhatsApp Cloud API to deliver the response to the customer.

This process allows multiple employees to manage customer communication without needing separate business phone numbers.

Can Multiple Agents Use One WhatsApp Business Number?

Yes. Multiple agents can handle conversations associated with one WhatsApp Business Platform phone number when the business uses a suitable shared inbox or customer service application.

For example, an online store might have five support agents working from different computers. All five can access the same customer communication system and handle assigned conversations.

Customers continue messaging the same business number, even when different employees respond.

This approach creates a consistent communication experience and makes it easier to maintain customer conversation history.

How Can Businesses Assign Chats to Different Agents?

Agent assignment is an important feature of a multi-agent support system.

A connected platform can provide different assignment methods depending on its capabilities.

Manual assignment: A supervisor selects an agent and assigns a conversation based on availability or expertise.

Automatic assignment: The platform distributes incoming conversations among available agents.

Department-based assignment: Messages are directed to specific teams, such as sales, billing, or technical support.

Round-robin assignment: New conversations are distributed between agents in rotation.

These methods help businesses organize incoming messages and prevent one employee from handling every customer request.

Can Multiple Agents Reply to the Same Customer?

Yes, depending on the connected platform's features and permissions. Multiple agents may be able to access the same conversation, but businesses should establish clear ownership rules.

For example, one agent can take responsibility for a conversation while another provides internal assistance.

A shared inbox may also include assignment indicators, internal notes, and conversation status updates. These features help prevent two employees from sending conflicting replies.

Clear ownership is particularly important when customers are discussing payments, complaints, or complicated service requests.

What Features Should a Multi-Agent WhatsApp Platform Include?

Businesses should evaluate the following features before selecting a platform that connects with WhatsApp Cloud API:

Shared inbox: Allows multiple agents to view customer conversations.

Agent assignment: Distributes chats among team members.

Role permissions: Controls what individual employees can access.

Internal notes: Allows agents to communicate without sending messages to customers.

Conversation history: Helps agents understand previous interactions.

Notifications: Alerts agents about incoming messages and updates.

Performance reports: Helps managers review response times and agent activity.

Team management: Organizes employees into departments or support groups.

These features make it easier to manage customer communication as the business grows.

Is WhatsApp Cloud API Suitable for Large Support Teams?

WhatsApp Cloud API can support business messaging operations for growing companies. However, the overall multi-agent experience depends on the application connected to it.

A small business might only need a shared inbox with basic assignment features. A larger organization may require department management, advanced permissions, reporting, CRM integration, and automated routing.

Businesses should also consider API usage costs, message policies, platform subscription fees, and technical requirements before choosing a solution.

What Are the Benefits of Using Multiple Agents?

Allowing several agents to manage WhatsApp conversations offers several practical advantages.

First, it helps businesses handle more incoming messages without depending on one employee. Second, conversations can be assigned to people with relevant knowledge. Third, managers can monitor support activities and identify workflow problems.

It also makes employee coordination easier because agents can access relevant conversation information through one system.

Conclusion

WhatsApp Cloud API can work with multiple agents when connected to a suitable shared inbox, CRM, or customer support platform. Although the API provides the messaging infrastructure, the connected application manages the multi-agent experience.

With features such as chat assignment, team permissions, conversation history, and internal notes, businesses can create an organized support environment. Choosing the right integration helps teams manage customer conversations efficiently while maintaining communication through a single WhatsApp Business number.

title: Build Your Own Proof Gatekeeper Loop: A Hands-On Tutorial
description:
In zkVerify's Agent Games, the Proof Gatekeeper track gives your agent 60 seconds per task: read a transfer condition, decide APPROVE or REJECT, and back the decision with a Groth16 proof your opponent — the platform — re-verifies. Before you build the public endpoint the arena requires, build the loop itself, locally, on your own machine. That is what this tutorial does, step by step: download the tournament's official circuit, implement the decision checks, generate and verify a proof, and run the one test that proves the circuit refuses to lie.

This is my second entry for the Creator Track of #AgentGames. My first article was a build log of the same loop; this one is the tutorial I wish I had before writing it — the commands, the code, and the measured numbers, so you can reproduce every step. You need Node.js and about ten minutes. No zero-knowledge background is required: the circuit is a black box you feed inputs and get a proof from.

One honest note up front: everything below ran locally. I have no live endpoint and have played no scored rounds. What follows is the loop, verified against the official artifacts — not a claim about the arena.

Step 1: Get the official artifacts

Everything starts at the tournament's circuit-info endpoint:

curl -s https://agentgames.zkverify.io/api/circuit-info

It returns the download URLs for the two artifacts plus the platform's registered verification-key hash. Download both files into a working directory:

  • gatekeeper.wasm — 1,755,820 bytes, the compiled circuit
  • gatekeeper_final.zkey — 309,750 bytes, the proving key

The circuit takes 13 inputs and exposes 13 public signals. The signal names were documented by probing the official wasm in @rday98's public repo, which I credit here — I verified the interface against the official wasm myself before trusting it, and the code in this tutorial is my own implementation. Keep the registered vkHash from the endpoint handy; it is the value your decision logic compares every incoming proof key against (mine starts 0x6b79c6…d77b0).

Step 2: Set up the project 

mkdir gatekeeper && cd gatekeeper
npm init -y
npm install snarkjs@0.7.6 js-sha3

snarkjs does the proving and verifying; js-sha3 gives us keccak-256 for turning task IDs into circuit inputs (Step 4). That is the whole dependency list.

Step 3: Write decide() — the seven checks

Every task is either a valid condition or one of six traps. Your decide() runs the checks in trap-priority order and returns a decision plus a reason code:

function decide(task, seenProofs) {
  if (task.proof_vk.toLowerCase() !== task.registered_vk.toLowerCase())
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'VK_SUBSTITUTION' };
  if (seenProofs.has(task.proof_tx))
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'PROOF_REUSED' };
  if (BigInt(task.public_balance) < BigInt(task.minimum))
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'THRESHOLD_MISMATCH' };
  if (BigInt(task.current_block) >= BigInt(task.expiry_block))
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'EXPIRED_CONDITION' };
  if (task.recipient.toLowerCase() !== task.condition_recipient.toLowerCase())
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'RECIPIENT_MISMATCH' };
  if (BigInt(task.amount) > BigInt(task.max_transfer))
    return { decision: 'REJECT', reason_code: 'AMOUNT_OVERFLOW' };
  return { decision: 'APPROVE', reason_code: 'VALID_CONDITION' };
}

The order is deliberate. The verification-key check comes first: if the proof was made under the wrong key, nothing else in the envelope matters. Proof reuse comes second because it is the cheapest correct answer in the whole loop — a lookup in seenProofs, a Set of proof references from earlier tasks, before any proving work happens. About 11% of tasks are replays, per the tournament's trap documentation, and reuse is the only trap you cannot catch by looking at a single envelope in isolation: it needs memory. The remaining four checks are plain field comparisons — balance against minimum, current block against expiry, recipient against recipient, amount against cap — and if all of them pass, the condition is valid.

Two details worth copying exactly: compare addresses and hashes case-insensitively (hex casing varies between sources), and compare amounts and blocks as BigInt, not as JS numbers, so large values never lose precision.

For a worked example, use a clean envelope: public balance 1,460 against a minimum of 1,000, amount 500 against a cap of 1,000, expiry block 19,842,201 against a current block of 19,832,000, recipient matching. decide() returns APPROVE / VALID_CONDITION.

Step 4: Build the circuit input

The prover needs the same thirteen fields as circuit inputs. Eleven are copies of the envelope; two need a small transformation:

function buildInput(task, decision) {
  const salt = '0x' + crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex');
  return {
    registeredVkHash: task.registered_vk,
    proofVkHash: task.proof_vk,
    minimum: String(task.minimum),
    publicBalance: String(task.public_balance),
    expiryBlock: String(task.expiry_block),
    currentBlock: String(task.current_block),
    recipient: task.recipient,
    conditionRecipient: task.condition_recipient,
    amount: String(task.amount),
    maxTransfer: String(task.max_transfer),
    decision: decision === 'APPROVE' ? '1' : '0',
    taskId: taskIdToField(task.task_id).toString(),
    salt,
  };
}

The taskId is the keccak-256 hash of the task-id string, reduced modulo the BN128 field prime — a one-liner with js-sha3:

const FIELD_PRIME = BigInt('21888242871839275222246405745257275088548364400416034343698204186575808495617');
function taskIdToField(taskId) {
  const h = '0x' + keccak_256(Buffer.from(String(taskId), 'utf8'));
  return BigInt(h) % FIELD_PRIME;
}

The salt is fresh random 32 bytes per proof. Pass numbers as strings: snarkjs handles big values through strings, and it keeps you out of JS-number trouble. The decision bit is '1' for APPROVE and '0' for REJECT — the circuit enforces that the bit matches the checks, which is exactly what Step 6 tests.

Step 5: Prove and verify locally

Three snarkjs calls are the whole loop:

const { proof, publicSignals } =
  await snarkjs.groth16.fullProve(input, 'gatekeeper.wasm', 'gatekeeper_final.zkey');
const vk = await snarkjs.zKey.exportVerificationKey('gatekeeper_final.zkey');
const ok = await snarkjs.groth16.verify(vk, publicSignals, proof);

Run it on the clean envelope from Step 3, then on a trap: the same envelope with the proof key swapped for a different hash (0xaaaa…aaaa), which decide() rejects as VK_SUBSTITUTION — and which still gets a proof, because a REJECT decision is a claim the circuit can verify too. Here is what I measured on 15 November 2026, every number from the run:

Case Decision Prove time Proof size Local verify
Valid condition APPROVE 1,581 ms 724 bytes OK in 37 ms
VK-substitution trap REJECT 488 ms 722 bytes OK in 96 ms
Reused proof reference REJECT — (decision only) — —

The first proof took 1,581 ms because it is cold: it includes loading the wasm and the zkey. The second, with everything warm, took 488 ms. Both proofs verified locally against the verification key exported from the official zkey, Groth16/BN128, 13 public signals. The reused-proof case never reached the prover at all — the seen-set caught it at the decision stage. The practical takeaway: proving costs well under two seconds even cold, a small fraction of the 60-second budget per task. The cryptography is not the bottleneck; the checks are the work.

Step 6: The lie test

Now the test that justifies the whole exercise. Take the VK-substitution trap — a task your logic correctly rejected — and force the decision bit to APPROVE anyway:

await proveAndVerify(buildInput(trappedTask, 'APPROVE'));

If the circuit is doing its job, there is no valid witness for that claim, and witness calculation must fail. It does:

Error: Assert Failed. Error in template GatekeeperEvaluation_79 line: 102

A lie has no valid witness. The constraint system refuses to produce a proof for a decision the inputs do not support — not because the agent is honest, but because the arithmetic will not cooperate. Run this test yourself: it is the fastest way to confirm your loop is wired to the real circuit and not to a stub that would happily prove anything.

Three gotchas

The registered vkHash is not a plain keccak-256 of the verification-key JSON. I tried both the compact and pretty-printed forms. The platform's hashing scheme is undocumented, so do not try to recompute the hash — take the value from /api/circuit-info as given and compare against it. The key itself is genuine: it comes from the official zkey, and proofs generated against it verify.

The seen-set must live across tasks. If you create a fresh Set per task, reuse detection silently stops working and replays sail through. Keep one set for the whole run (or the whole round) and add each proof reference after deciding.

Fail closed by construction. The check order in Step 3 already does this: anything unrecognized or unparseable should fall through to a REJECT, never to an APPROVE. A gatekeeper that approves on uncertainty is a gatekeeper waiting for its first wrong APPROVE.

Where this stops

You now have a loop that decides, proves, and verifies — locally, against the tournament's real circuit. What it is not: a live endpoint, a scored round, or a finished entry. The arena requires a public HTTPS endpoint the platform can reach, and that is a separate build (for me, still an open problem: the machine I work on has no public IP). But the loop is the part you can perfect offline, and every trap in the tournament is decided here, in decide(), long before any proof is generated.

I registered for the tournament as handle saimlu via wallet sign-in (SIWE) using an EOA wallet. If you reproduce this loop and find a trap case I missed, or a cleaner way to build the input, that is exactly the kind of thing the Creator Track is for — write it up.

Links

  • Agent Games: https://agentgames.zkverify.io
  • Builder Field Guide: https://agentgames.zkverify.io/build
  • Proof Gatekeeper track: https://agentgames.zkverify.io/events/proof-gatekeeper
  • Circuit info (official artifacts): https://agentgames.zkverify.io/api/circuit-info
  • snarkjs: https://github.com/iden3/snarkjs
  • Circuit-interface probing credited to @rday98's public repo.

title: What Is an Agent-Native Operating System?
description:
"AI operating system" has quietly become one of the most overloaded phrases in software. It
gets stuck on chat apps, on developer frameworks, on browser extensions, on anything with a
language model somewhere inside it. So it's worth being precise about what an agent-native
operating system actually is — because the distinction isn't marketing, it's architectural,
and it changes what the software can promise you.

The one-line version: AI as the OS, not AI on the OS. In an agent-native OS, the agent
is the interface you log into, and the traditional desktop — the compositor, the window
manager, the app model, the tray of background daemons — is gone, not decorated. This post
lays out what that means, how it differs from the AI features being bolted onto everything
else, and why the operating-system layer is the right place for it.

Start with what today's OS is actually for

Look at where a modern desktop spends its budget — RAM, CPU, attention, attack surface. Almost
all of it goes to helping a human drive a fleet of applications with a mouse and keyboard:
a compositor to draw overlapping windows, a window manager to arrange them, an application
model so programs can be launched and switched, and a constellation of background services to
keep it all humming. For forty years that was exactly right. The human was the intelligence in
the loop; the machine's job was to render windows and get out of the way.

An agent inverts that arrangement. The agent is now the thing doing the driving — perceiving,
deciding, acting. But it's being asked to drive through an interface built on the assumption
that a careful human is at the wheel. That mismatch is the whole reason "put an AI in the
sidebar" never quite feels like the future: you've added an intelligent driver to a car
designed to be driven by hand, and left all the manual controls in place.

The three things that make an OS "agent-native"

An agent-native OS isn't a desktop with an assistant added. It's a different set of primitives.
Three properties separate the real thing from the retrofit.

1. The agent is the surface, not a feature. You log in from your display manager into the
OS itself and talk to the agent. There's no launcher, no grid of app icons, no "open the
assistant" step — because there's nothing else to open. The agent is what you're using. That's
the literal meaning of agent-native: the agent is native to the system, not hosted by it.

2. Delivery windows replace application windows. When the agent does work, it renders that
work into typed panes, cards, and streams it opens, fills, and closes as it goes — delivery
windows, not application windows you operate.
You're watching work be delivered, not driving a toolbar. The unit of the interface shifts from
"an app you run" to "a result the agent produces."

3. Authority is brokered, not ambient. This is the deepest difference and the easiest to
miss. On a normal OS, a program acts with the ambient authority of whoever launched it — if
you can do it, the program can do it, up to and including a raw shell and sudo. That's
tolerable when a careful human is deciding what runs. It's the whole problem when the thing
deciding is a probabilistic model that can be wrong or manipulated. An agent-native OS instead
routes every consequential action through a typed capability
broker with a default-deny policy:
the agent presents a token for exactly the authority a task needs, and holds nothing more. The
shell never bypasses it. (Why that belongs in the OS, not the
app.)

What you get when those three hold

Those primitives aren't ends in themselves — they're what make a set of otherwise-unreasonable
promises actually keepable:

  • Inspectable. Every plan, tool call, approval, and result is logged, timestamped, and replayable. Agent work stops being write-only.
  • Trustworthy. No raw shell, no raw sudo; consequential actions pass the broker. Least privilege and containment are properties of the system, not promises of an app.
  • Local-first. The default is a model on your own machine, with hosted models on tap rather than on the critical path — so your files and context don't have to leave to get work done.
  • Durable. Sessions survive a reboot. The record of what happened is still there tomorrow.

Notice that every one of those is a statement about the environment the agent runs in. You
cannot bolt them onto an app, because the app doesn't control the environment — the OS does.
That's the argument for doing this at the operating-system layer instead of as one more
assistant in one more sidebar.

How it differs from the things it gets confused with

  • An AI assistant / copilot is an application that runs on your OS and helps you drive other applications. Useful, but it inherits the desktop's assumptions and its ambient authority. Agent-native means there's no "other applications" tier to drive.
  • An agent framework or SDK is a toolkit for developers to build agents. It's a library, not the system you log into. An agent-native OS is the runtime and the surface, not the scaffolding.
  • A chat app with tools is a conversation with function-calling attached. It has no OS-level authority model, no durable session at the system level, and no replaceable desktop — the three things that define the category.

If a product keeps the app model and adds intelligence, it's AI on the OS. If it deletes the
app model and makes the agent the system, it's AI as the OS. Only the second is agent-native.

Being honest about the phase

Categories get oversold, so here's the phase-honest version. Building this is staged. The
alpha replaces your desktop session — you log into the agent-native OS instead of GNOME or
KDE — while your machine keeps its kernel. It ships the runtime, the typed broker, a reference
agentic shell, and a display-manager session entry, as a package on Debian/Ubuntu. The later,
larger step is a full distribution with the compositor and desktop stack gone at the image
level. We're building it in the open, in Rust, under Apache 2.0, and we'd rather describe the
destination precisely than pretend we're already standing on it.

So: an agent-native operating system is one where the agent is the surface, delivery windows
replace application windows, and authority is brokered instead of ambient — which together make
an inspectable, trustworthy, local-first, durable system possible. It's for people who'd rather
drive their machine through an agent than through a grid of app icons. Everything else in this
blog is a closer look at one of those pillars.

MagenticOS is built by Mutagenic Labs, LLC. Open source, Apache 2.0.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/what-is-an-agent-native-operating-system. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Testing AI Agents: Why Unit Tests Aren't Enough
description:
You ship a change to your agent's system prompt. You run the tests. They pass. You deploy.

Three days later, your support agent starts filing refund requests as generic support tickets. The prompts look fine. The code looks fine. Nothing broke — except the part that matters.

This is the testing gap in AI systems. Traditional unit tests are still essential, but they don't tell you whether your agent behaves correctly across the range of inputs your users will send.

You need something else: evaluation tests, or evals.

Why Unit Tests Aren't Enough

A unit test checks deterministic behavior:

expect(parse_date("march 20", today: Date.new(2026, 1, 15))).to eq("2026-03-20")

Call it a thousand times, get the same result a thousand times. Any deviation is a bug. (Note the pinned today: — without it, even this test changes answer on January 1st.)

An LLM call is different. It's a probabilistic system. Given the same input, it generates a likely output — not necessarily an identical one. Sampling parameters influence this behavior, and even with temperature: 0, hosted models can produce slightly different results between runs.

The naive approach — run the agent and assert its output — fails in two ways:

  • False failures: The output is semantically correct but formatted slightly differently. Your test breaks on a Tuesday.
  • False passes: The output passes your specific assertion, but the model has regressed on cases you never tested.

Unit tests can verify the code around an LLM. They cannot, by themselves, establish that the model behaves correctly. You have to evaluate it.

What You're Actually Testing

When an agent processes a message, there are three distinct things that can go wrong:

1. The noop decision. Did the agent correctly decide to act — or not act?

"cn u snd towles to rom 305 thx" → should trigger an action.

"👍" → should not.

Getting this wrong is expensive: false positives flood your backend with phantom events, while false negatives silently drop real requests.

2. The action type. Did the agent pick the right action from the allowed list?

"My order ORD-8832 arrived damaged" should produce support.refund.process, not support.ticket.create. Both are valid action types. Only one is correct.

3. Field extraction. Did the agent extract the right information from the message?

booking_ref: "AB1234"
new_date: "2026-03-20"

These are the values your backend acts on. A wrong date changes a booking to the wrong day. A missing order ID stalls a refund.

A single pass/fail assertion can't tell you which of these three failed.

The Eval Dataset

An eval suite starts with a labeled dataset. Each case represents a realistic input with an explicit expected output:

- id: h05
  tags: [typo]
  message: "i nee to chaneg my bokking to april 3rd plz ref XY789"
  expected:
    action_type: hospitality.booking.modify
    noop: false
    fields:
      booking_ref: "XY789"
      new_date: "2026-04-03"

One detail that bites later: "april 3rd" only means 2026-04-03 relative to a reference date. Pin that date and pass it to the agent on every run, or your expected values silently rot when the calendar moves.

The tags are important. You don't just want a pass rate — you want to know where the model struggles.

For example:

Tag What it tests
clean Well-formed messages — the baseline
typo Spelling errors, autocorrect, missing vowels
emoji Heavy emoji usage
multilang French, Spanish, German mixed with English
ambiguous Multiple valid interpretations
implicit Intent not stated directly
multi_intent Two requests in one message
noop Should produce no action
context Follow-up requiring previous conversation state

The ambiguous and implicit tags are often where gaps appear first.

"The room is too cold" — is this a room service request, or just a complaint? (ambiguous)

"I don't think I'll make it" — is this a cancellation? (implicit)

Clean examples almost always pass. The interesting failures are the ones that look like real user messages.

The Scoring Model

The runner iterates over every case, calls the agent, and evaluates its output across three axes.

For repeatability, we use temperature: 0. This reduces sampling variability, but does not guarantee identical outputs across runs, especially when using hosted APIs.

Here's a simplified evaluator:

def evaluate(expected, output)
  errors = []

  # Axis 1: noop detection
  expected_noop = expected["noop"] == true
  actual_noop = noop_output?(output)

  unless expected_noop == actual_noop
    errors << "noop: expected=#{expected_noop}, got=#{actual_noop}"
  end

  # Axis 2: action type
  unless expected_noop
    expected_type = expected["action_type"]
    actual_type = extract_action_type(output)

    unless expected_type == actual_type
      errors << "action_type: expected=#{expected_type}, got=#{actual_type}"
    end
  end

  # Axis 3: field presence
  if expected["fields"]
    check_fields(expected["fields"], output, errors)
  end

  { pass: errors.empty?, errors: errors }
end

def check_fields(expected_fields, output, errors)
  actual = output.fetch("fields", {})

  expected_fields.each_key do |name|
    value = actual[name]
    errors << "fields.#{name}: missing" if value.nil? || value.to_s.strip.empty?
  end
end

Notice what we don't do here: exact value matching on every field. We start by checking field presence.

Why? Because different representations can express the same information. For example, "march 20" and "2026-03-20" may represent the same date. Exact equality would require normalization rules for each field type.

But there's an important trade-off. A presence check won't catch a wrong date. It only catches missing information. For fields that directly influence business operations — dates, amounts, IDs — value validation is essential.

A practical approach is to start with presence checks, then add field-specific validation and normalization as the system evolves. The goal isn't to make every assertion complicated. It's to catch the failures that matter.

Why not use an LLM as a judge? Because the output here is structured: a noop flag, an action type, a set of fields. Deterministic checks are free, fast, and don't add a second source of variance. A judge earns its place when the output is free text.

Baselines and Regression Detection

After each run, save the results to a timestamped file:

spec/eval/results/
  20260307_baseline.yml
  20260308_224748_support_recheck.yml
  20260309_122811_gemini-2.0-flash.yml

The label matters. You're not looking at a single score — you're tracking a trajectory. (All runs in this article date from March 2026; model names and prices reflect that period.)

For example:

# 20260307_baseline.yml
scores:
  action_type: 95.8
  fields: 85.7

These scores become your behavioral baseline. Break them down by tag too: a global score hides most of the signal, and a drop on multilang alone tells you far more than a one-point dip overall.

Improve the system prompt? Run the eval. Scores hold or improve → good sign. Scores drop significantly, or a category that previously scored 100% starts failing → investigate.

Don't treat every small variation as a regression. Hosted models exhibit run-to-run variance, so measure it: run the same configuration a few times and note how much the scores move on their own. Anything inside that spread is noise.

The key discipline:

Always run the eval before merging a change that affects model behavior.

A diff on a YAML prompt file won't tell you if you just broke field extraction on multilingual inputs.

CI integration is useful, but optional. Running the suite consistently matters more than automating it immediately.

What the Failures Teach You

The first baseline surfaced 10 failures. The patterns were instructive.

Ambiguous cases fail predictably.

"The room is too cold" produced no action at all. The model wasn't confident enough to commit to hospitality.room_service.request without more signals.

This isn't necessarily a bug. It's a calibration question: do you want confident-only extractions or best-effort behavior?

Fields fail on implicit mentions.

"✅ driver karim delivered everything in nice 🏁"

The model got the action type right (operations.driver.update) but missed destination: Nice. "Nice" is a city, but also an adjective. Field extraction on ambiguous proper nouns is genuinely hard.

Cross-domain routing underperforms.

"Cancel my booking ref HT9921 and also where is my order ORD-5500?"

The expected behavior is to route to both the hospitality and the support domains. The model picked one. Multi-intent cross-domain routing is a difficult case: a single model call has to recognize and preserve multiple intents.

These failures tell you exactly what to work on next — and give you a metric to validate whether your fix actually worked.

As the system evolves, the dataset should evolve too. Add new cases from production failures, edge cases and unexpected user behavior. Otherwise, your eval suite gradually becomes a collection of examples the model already knows how to handle.

The Cost Argument

Here's what makes this approach sustainable:

98 cases × gpt-4o-mini = $0.0106

Just over one cent for a full behavioral evaluation suite, based on the model and pricing used for this run. You can run it after every prompt change, every model swap, or every meaningful pipeline update.

Want to evaluate a different model — say, switching from gpt-4o-mini to gemini-2.0-flash? Run the same dataset against both and compare:

# gpt-4o-mini
scores:
  action_type: 95.8
  fields: 85.7

# gemini-2.0-flash
scores:
  action_type: 94.1
  fields: 83.2

The honest reading: on this dataset, a 1.7-point gap on action type is one or two cases — well within run-to-run variance. These two models are equivalent here, so the decision comes down to cost and latency. That's still a useful answer, and one you couldn't get from a gut feeling.

The exact cost will depend on model pricing, input size and output tokens, but the point remains: a small, focused eval suite can be surprisingly cheap.

Unit Tests, Evals and Integration Tests

These three testing approaches solve different problems.

  • Unit tests verify that your deterministic code works: parsing, validation, permissions and business logic.
  • Evals measure whether the model produces the expected behavior across a representative dataset.
  • Integration tests verify that the generated output works correctly within the rest of your system.

None replaces the others. A correctly classified request doesn't guarantee that the resulting action will execute successfully. Likewise, a passing integration test doesn't prove that the model will classify the next 100 user messages correctly.

The Pattern

Distilled, the approach looks like this:

  1. Build a dataset of realistic inputs with tagged categories
  2. Define scoring dimensions, not just pass/fail
  3. Save results after every significant change
  4. Protect the baseline and measure run-to-run variance
  5. Add new cases from real failures and edge cases
  6. Use the results to prioritize what to fix next

No framework required. It's a dataset, a runner, and a disciplined habit of checking model behavior before shipping changes.

Traditional tests tell you whether your code works. Evals tell you whether your AI system does what you expect.

The teams that skip this often discover regressions only after a user reports them. By then, you don't know which change caused the problem, and you're debugging blind.

If your AI system is important enough to ship, its behavior is important enough to test.

title: The Sandbox Is the Wrong Unit for AI Agents
description:
Every serious agent product now ships with a sandbox. Container, VM, namespace, seccomp profile, a browser in a browser. The pitch is the same everywhere: the agent runs in there, so whatever it does, it can't hurt you.

That claim is true in exactly the way it was true for the programs sandboxes were built for, and false in the way that matters for agents. An AI agent sandbox protects the host from the process. It does not protect you from the agent's decisions, because the decisions are the product, and the sandbox was never designed to see them.

What a sandbox was built to answer

Process isolation answers one question well: what can this program touch? Namespaces decide which filesystem, network, and process tree the program sees. Seccomp decides which system calls it may make. A container image decides which binaries exist at all. Draw the box, drop the program in, and the box holds regardless of what the program does inside it.

That model has an assumption baked so deep that nobody says it out loud: the program's behaviour is fixed before it runs. You know what ffmpeg does. You know what the payment worker does. The sandbox exists because you don't fully trust the implementation, so you bound the blast radius of bugs and of hostile input. The intent is not in question; the code's fidelity to the intent is.

An agent inverts that. The implementation is fine. The intent is decided at runtime, one step at a time, by a model reading whatever landed in its context. The agent that was supposed to summarize a folder decides, three steps in, that the summary would be better if it also emailed the folder to the person it thinks asked for it. Nothing in that sequence is a bug. Nothing escaped. The sandbox held perfectly, and it held around the wrong thing.

The failure mode is not escape

Look at the agent incidents people actually report. The duplicate purchase after a timeout. The repository force-pushed over. The calendar cleared because "reschedule" was read as "remove." The support reply that promised a refund the policy doesn't allow. The file shared with the whole org instead of one person.

Not one of these is a sandbox escape. Every one of them was a permitted action, taken by a process inside its box, using credentials that were legitimately available to it, doing something the box was never asked to prevent. Isolation was never the control that would have caught them, because isolation controls reach, and these were failures of judgment within reach.

That is the quiet compromise: we have accepted "it can't get out" as a proxy for "it won't do the wrong thing," when the two are not even about the same layer. The first is a property of the process. The second is a property of each action.

Why the box is the wrong size

Try to fix this with the sandbox and you find out why it is the wrong unit.

It is all-or-nothing per process. A sandbox grants the process a set of reach at start-up. Either the network is there or it isn't; either the directory is mounted or it isn't. An agent that needs to read one file to plan and write one different file to finish does not have a per-process shape. Its needs are per-step, and they are not known before the process starts. So the box gets drawn around the union of everything the agent might need, which is the same thing as not drawing a box.

It has no notion of intent. The sandbox sees a connect() and a write(). It cannot distinguish the email the user asked for from the email the agent decided to send. Both are the same syscall on the same socket. The information that would separate them, what the user requested and what the agent is trying to accomplish, exists only in the agent's context, which the sandbox cannot read and should not trust anyway.

It does not know who is acting. Inside the box there is one process identity. It does not carry "on behalf of whom" or "under which task." So there is nothing to revoke when a task ends, nothing to scope when a task begins, and nothing in the record afterwards that says which decision produced which side effect. The box's own logs, if any, say a process did a thing.

It leaks around the edges by design. Agents are useful precisely because they touch the systems we care about: mail, calendars, repositories, payment APIs, the actual filesystem. The sandbox that genuinely prevented all of that would be a sandbox around a toy. So every real deployment punches the holes the agent needs, and the holes are where the incidents happen.

None of this means sandboxes are bad. They are still the right answer to their own question. Run agent tool code in one; keep the blast radius of a bad dependency small. But defence-in-depth around the process is not the same as a control on the action, and calling the first the second is how teams end up with an incident report that says "the sandbox worked" on the same page as "the customer was charged twice."

The unit that fits is the action

If the agent's behaviour is decided one step at a time, then the boundary has to be checkable one step at a time. The unit of isolation for an agent is not the process. It is the action: this operation, on this resource, on behalf of this principal, under this task, right now.

That reframing changes what the questions are:

  • Not "can this process reach the network?" but "may this action send this message to this recipient?"
  • Not "is the directory mounted?" but "may this task write this file, and is that write the one the plan said it would make?"
  • Not "which user is the process running as?" but "which task is asking, on whose authority, and will the record show it?"

Answering those requires three properties that a per-process sandbox structurally cannot supply. Authority has to be typed and granted per action rather than per process, default-deny, so that "read one file" and "send one email" are different grants rather than the same open door. Every action has to pass through a single point that can see the request, not the syscall, so that intent-level checks are even possible. And the point that mediates the action has to write the record, so that what happened is attributable to a task and a decision, not to a process ID.

Those are operating-system responsibilities. Not because the OS is the only place they could live, but because it is the only place that sees every action regardless of which app, framework, or model produced it. A framework can add a permission prompt to its own tool calls. A model provider can add a refusal. Neither sees the action the other one took, and neither is still in the loop when the agent shells out to a script that does the real work. The layer beneath all of them is.

What this looks like from the outside

Picture the same "summarize a folder" task in an arrangement where the action is the unit. The task starts with authority to read that folder and write one summary file, and nothing else. Three steps in, the agent decides to email the folder. That decision is not blocked by a rule in a prompt; there is simply no grant that covers it, so the action cannot be issued. If the user wants it, the grant is a deliberate, visible act, scoped to that task, and it expires when the task does. Afterwards the record shows the reads, the one write, and the attempted send that had no authority, each tied to the task that produced it.

Nothing about that requires the model to be better behaved. It requires the surrounding system to stop treating the process as the thing it trusts or distrusts, and start treating each action as the thing it decides about.

Where we are with it

We are building toward exactly this arrangement, and we are in alpha. The honest description of the alpha is a runtime with a typed capability layer and a reference shell, running local-first, with the sandbox still present underneath as defence-in-depth rather than as the control. Much of what a mature system would do at the action boundary is still ahead of us, and some of what we have is rough. What is settled is the unit. Draw the box around the process and you have protected the host from the code. Draw it around the action and you have protected the person from the decision. Agents are made of decisions.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/sandbox-is-the-wrong-unit-for-ai-agents. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Capability-Based Security for AI Agents
description:
Ask yourself what an AI agent on your machine is actually allowed to do. Not what you'd like it to do — what the system will permit if the agent tries. On almost every setup in use today, the honest answer is: whatever you're allowed to do. The agent runs inside a process that runs as you, and "you" is a very large grant. Capability-based security for AI agents is the argument that this is the wrong trust model at its root — that an agent should start with the authority to do nothing, and receive narrow, typed, revocable grants for exactly the actions its task requires. It's an old idea in operating systems research. The actor it was waiting for has finally arrived.

The app-permission model assumes a human is driving

The permission model everyone actually lives under was designed around two comfortable assumptions: the unit of trust is the application, and the entity driving it is a person.

So the questions the system asks are app-shaped and person-shaped. "Allow this app to access your files?" "Allow this app to use the network?" You answer once, usually at install time, usually yes, and the grant persists forever at the granularity of an entire program. From then on, the app operates with what security people call ambient authority — it doesn't present credentials for each action; it simply acts, and the system checks whether you could have done it. Since you can do nearly everything, so can it.

This was always a coarse arrangement, but it held together because of the second assumption: a human was in the loop, clicking each button, more or less aware of what was happening. The app's authority was broad, but its actions were throttled by human attention. The grant was the size of a barn door, and a person walked through it one step at a time.

The actor changed. The model didn't.

Now put an agent in the driver's seat and watch both assumptions fail at once.

An agent is not throttled by human attention — issuing actions at machine speed is its entire value. And an agent is not a fixed program whose behavior you can audit once and trust forever; it's a probabilistic system whose next action depends on its context, which includes text it read five minutes ago from a source you've never vetted. The security community has a growing catalog of what follows — OWASP's Top 10 for LLM applications puts prompt injection and "excessive agency" near the top, and excessive agency is really just ambient authority wearing its new name.

The classic term for the resulting failure is the confused deputy: a program with legitimate authority tricked into using it for someone else's ends. Agents are the most confusable deputies ever built. They can be instructed by anything that can get words in front of them. Hand a confusable actor your full ambient authority and you haven't built an assistant-shaped tool; you've built a very fast intern with your keys, your badge, and a habit of taking directions from strangers.

The industry's current answer is supervision — watch every step, approve every action. That works, at the cost of the thing you wanted, which was delegation. All-or-nothing trust gives you exactly two settings: babysit, or hope. Neither is a security model. Both are coping strategies for a permission system that has no vocabulary for the thing we're now asking it to govern.

What capability-based security gets right

Capability systems invert the model's core assumption. Instead of an actor carrying broad ambient authority checked against an identity, authority lives in capabilities: unforgeable tokens that each designate a specific resource together with specific rights over it. If you hold the capability, you can perform the action. If you don't, there is no action to attempt — the request isn't denied so much as impossible to express.

Three properties follow, and each one lands directly on the agent problem.

Default-deny. An actor begins with nothing. Every authority it holds was explicitly granted, which means the complete answer to "what can this agent do?" is "here is the list of what it was handed" — a list you can read, rather than a subtraction problem over everything your account can reach. Least privilege stops being an aspiration written in a policy document and becomes a structural fact.
