  • Write the result you sell in one sentence. It should not be "AI images" or "AI text".
  • Ask the one-prompt question: could the buyer get this alone?
  • Make samples from material you own. Fiverr's help center says to use images you own, with no copyrighted material or images sourced from the internet.
  • Prepare one case study or before-and-after example (Upwork's advice to freelancers).
  • Read Fiverr's Gig policies and Prohibited Services guidelines before you create a Gig.
  • Use a desktop browser for a Fiverr Gig. It cannot be created on mobile.
  • Have identity and tax details ready. Fiverr asks for them before you publish, and Upwork may ask you to confirm identifying information when you start a proposal.
  • Remember that Fiverr's numbers are search growth, not hires.
  • Check the dates. Both reports compare periods that ended in April 2026 (Fiverr) and Q1 2026 (Upwork's platform data).

What the numbers do not tell you

  • Fiverr's numbers are search growth, not hires.
  • Upwork's survey is about U.S. workers.
  • Upwork classifies AI jobs with an LLM-based pipeline, and says itself: "there is great uncertainty with measuring AI work."
  • Neither report gives dollar earnings for any side hustle.

But both reports point the same way.

And one more number from Upwork.
Skilled freelancers are now 38% of U.S. knowledge workers, up from 28% the year before.
58% of full-time employees say they are considering freelancing, up from 36%.

More people are coming.
The easy AI work will get more crowded, not less.

AI did not make side hustles easy.
It made judgment the thing people pay for.

Sources (official pages, read November 6, 2026):

  • Upwork, "Upwork's Future Workforce Index 2026" press release, July 14, 2026 (upwork.com/press)
  • Upwork Research Institute, "The Future Workforce Index 2026: AI, Freelancing, and the New Value of Work" (upwork.com/research/research-future-workforce-index-2026)
  • Fiverr, "Businesses Race to Hire Claude Code Specialists As Demand Surges 938%", GlobeNewswire, June 9, 2026
  • Fiverr Help Center, "Creating a Gig" (help.fiverr.com)
  • Upwork Help Center, "How to create a project in Project Catalog" and "How to submit a proposal on Upwork" (support.upwork.com)

title: AskDB: AI-written SQL and charts, without AI seeing your data
description:
People want to use AI to run reports on their databases. They also don't want to give AI access to their database. It's a Catch-22.

AskDB is an open-source TypeScript text-to-SQL toolkit: it turns a question into checked SQL for your app to run. The model sees your schema and the notes you write, never your data.

Today I'm announcing the release candidate for AskDB 1.0. The current build is 1.0.0-rc.3.

The whole flow in 41 seconds: watch the demo.

Where NL-to-SQL goes wrong

NL-to-SQL is an old problem. Systems that answer English questions from a database go back to BASEBALL (1961)1 and LUNAR (1971)2. Studies of large language models such as OpenAI's Codex writing SQL go back to early 20223. So the problem is not new.

The problem now isn't generating plausible SQL. It's conveying all the business context, terms and lingo consistently, so the AI generates SQL that's correct, not just plausible. It's in what the schema doesn't say, and in what the LLM assumes or hallucinates.

For example: a model that sees orders.total_amount integer doesn't know the amount is stored in cents. It doesn't know that when your finance team says "sales" they mean paid orders, not every order. Those facts live in people's heads, or have to be explained to the model every time someone asks a question.

What you want is to write those nuances down once, as notes on the schema, keep them in version control where you can keep improving them, and have them reach the model the same way on every question. That's what AskDB does.

What that looks like

Here's a snippet of a schema from the repo's test fixtures. The orders table has no sales column. "Sales" is a business word, defined in the schema's Markdown. Here's part of tables/orders.md:

---
id: table:public.orders
name: orders
...
columns:
  - id: table:public.orders#total_amount
    aliases: [revenue, sale_amount]
    description: Stored in cents. Use `total_amount / 100.0` for dollar values.
  ...
---

## Common query language

- "sales" usually means paid orders (`status = 'paid'`)
- "revenue" usually means `sum(total_amount)` where `status = 'paid'`

The question is "How much did we make in sales, in dollars?" This is the schema part of the prompt AskDB built for it:

The prompt as text 
Database schema:
TABLE public.users -- aliases: accounts, members
-- Registered user accounts. One row per signed-up user.
  - id uuid (PK NOT NULL) -- aliases: user_id
  - email text (NOT NULL) (sensitive)
  - created_at timestamptz (NOT NULL) -- aliases: signup_date, registered_at; When the user account was created.
-- common query language --
-- - "users" and "members" refer to this table
-- - "new users" usually means accounts created in the selected date range
-- - "active users" typically means users who placed at least one order
-- business context --
-- Each user has a unique email address used for login. The `email` column is sensitive — filter on it only when necessary and never display it in group-by reports.

TABLE public.orders -- aliases: purchases, sales, transactions
-- Customer purchase orders. One row per submitted order.
  - id uuid (PK NOT NULL) -- aliases: order_id
  - user_id uuid (NOT NULL)
  - status text (NOT NULL) -- aliases: order_status; values: pending|paid|shipped|cancelled; Order lifecycle state. Most reporting filters on `paid`.
  - total_amount integer (NOT NULL) -- aliases: revenue, sale_amount; Stored in cents. Use `total_amount / 100.0` for dollar values.
  FK (user_id) -> public.users (id)
-- common query language --
-- - "sales" usually means paid orders (`status = 'paid'`)
-- - "revenue" usually means `sum(total_amount)` where `status = 'paid'`
-- - "new orders" usually means orders created in the selected date range
-- business context --
-- Orders move through `pending → paid → shipped` and may end in `cancelled`. The `total_amount` column is stored in cents.

-- concepts --
-- Customer; synonyms: user, client, buyer, account holder; links: public.users; A person who has signed up and placed at least one order.
-- Revenue; synonyms: sales, gross sales, top line; links: public.orders.total_amount; Sum of `orders.total_amount` where `status = 'paid'`, expressed in cents.

Question: How much did we make in sales, in dollars?

It isn't DDL or SQL. It's a condensed format of the tables and the notes written about them.

Everything the model needs is in that text: "sales" means paid, and amounts are in cents. Concepts that span more than one table, like the Revenue concept at the bottom, come from a second file, concepts.md.

The call is one function in @askdb/core:

import { ask, loadSchema } from "@askdb/core";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

const result = await ask({
  question: "How much did we make in sales, in dollars?",
  schema: loadSchema("./schema"), // the schema artifact directory
  dialect: "postgres",
  model: openai("gpt-4o-mini"), // any Vercel AI SDK model object
});

With @askdb/core 1.0.0-rc.3 and OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini, it returned this (trimmed):

{
  "sql": "SELECT SUM(total_amount) / 100.0 AS sales_in_dollars\nFROM public.orders\nWHERE status = 'paid';",
  "verdict": {
    "outcome": "allow",
    "findings": []
  },
  "sensitiveGuardrail": {
    "passed": true,
    "references": []
  },
  "unboundSql": "SELECT SUM(total_amount) / 100.0 AS sales_in_dollars\nFROM public.orders\nWHERE status = $1;",
  "params": ["paid"]
}

The model divided by 100 and filtered on paid because the notes told it to. unboundSql and params are the same query with its values pulled out, ready for your driver to bind.

The verdict comes from AskDB's checks, which run on every SQL string before your code sees it.

The schema artifact

AskDB keeps what it knows about your database in one directory, the schema artifact. It has two layers.

The physical layer (schema.json): the tables, columns, types, keys and relationships. askdb introspect writes it by reading the database catalogs (information_schema, pg_catalog, sys.*, sqlite_master). Introspection collects no sample values.

The enrichment layer (the Markdown files): one file per table or concept you choose to describe, written by people. You can write those files by hand or in Studio (more on that below). Because it's all files, your data team reviews a change to "what sales means" in a pull request, and you can see line by line what the model will receive.

The physical layer is enough for SQL that runs. The enrichment layer is what makes it right for the business. Without the two notes above, the model could just as well have summed every order and reported cents as dollars: valid SQL, wrong answer.

When you ask a question, AskDB folds the two layers into the compact text you saw above and sends it to the model with your question. It holds back the notes on any sensitive table or column, and the example questions, which are there for retrieval.

A large schema is too big to send whole on every question. Past about 22 tables, or when the rendered schema routinely passes 8K tokens, turn on retrieval with @askdb/rag. It indexes the same artifact in a vector store and puts only the relevant slice into each prompt. @askdb/rag stays on 0.x at 1.0, so its API may still move.

ask() takes no database connection, so it never sees your rows or query results and can't send them. Introspection connects only at build time to read the catalogs. It sends nothing to a model. A value reaches the prompt only as text you wrote into the artifact, such as an enum list, or text the user typed in the question. Two caveats. Anything you write in the Markdown goes to the model verbatim. A label you pass in tenantScope.context, such as a customer's name, goes into the prompt as written too. And as you'd expect, retrieval adds a second provider: your embedding model receives every schema chunk when you build the index, and the question on each call.

Studio: enrich and test before you ship

You don't have to write the Markdown by hand. npx askdb studio opens AskDB Studio, a local web app on your machine that reads and writes the schema artifact directly. It's where I'd start: describe a table, add its aliases and common query language, then ask a question in the Playground and read the SQL and its check results. If the SQL isn't what you expected, tighten the notes and ask again, without leaving the tab. That loop (enrich, ask, re-enrich) is how you get reliable SQL for the words your team uses, before any of it touches your application.

Studio can also draft descriptions and aliases with your model for you to confirm. For a draft, it sends the model the table's column definitions and the names of up to four linked tables. Running the Playground's SQL against your database is off by default; turning it on means giving Studio a read-only role. Studio is still on 0.x at 1.0, so its UI may change. The Studio tour walks through every view.

When retrieval leaves out a table

Retrieval puts a table in the prompt only when one of the chunks it returns points to that table. Writing this blog, I hit the failure that follows from that.

On a made-up 63-table SaaS schema, I asked "What's our monthly recurring revenue from active subscriptions?" Only subscriptions was described, with the rule for an active subscription. Retrieval returned chunks from subscriptions, usage_records and subscription_events. It didn't return plans, where the prices live. The model never saw a price, so it counted the active subscriptions and multiplied by 10. The answer was $20. The right answer was $38. The SQL was a valid read-only query, so every check passed.

The fix was two files:

  1. tables/plans.md gave the table a description, aliases such as "subscription plans" and a business-context line saying MRR is built from plans.monthly_price.
  2. concepts.md got a monthly recurring revenue concept that links subscriptions and plans; when retrieval returns a concept, AskDB puts every table it links into the prompt. After re-indexing, the concept and the plans notes ranked first, and three runs out of three joined plans and returned 38.

The lesson is the same one the checks teach: they test the query's shape, not its numbers. Test the questions your users ask. The tutorial Find the right tables in a large schema walks through this case with the real output.

Your app runs the SQL

The library, the CLI and the HTTP API return SQL and never execute it. Your application runs it under its own database role. The one exception is Studio's Playground Execute button, a local development tool that's off by default.

I made this choice because the database role you already trust to run queries should be what bounds generated SQL. AskDB doesn't host inference either: you bring the model and the key, and it doesn't proxy, log or cache the requests. Use one of @askdb/ai's built-in providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Vercel AI Gateway) or pass any Vercel AI SDK model object to ask(). @askdb/ai uses the Vercel AI SDK under the hood, so the choice is between passing in the model your app already uses and letting @askdb/ai build one from your AskDB config.

The three checks

AskDB runs three checks on the returned SQL before passing it back to you:

  1. The read-only check, on for every built-in dialect. It makes sure no data-changing statement (UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE and the like) comes back.
  2. The tenant check, on when the schema has a tenant-policy.md and the caller's scope isn't global.
  3. The sensitive check, on when something is marked sensitive.

To show refusals, I stubbed the model to return SQL I wrote. The errors below are AskDB's real output on rc.3.

DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';:

{
  "name": "SqlValidationError",
  "message": "SQL must start with SELECT or WITH (got 'delete').",
  "verdict": {
    "outcome": "deny",
    "findings": [
      {
        "check": "read-only",
        "form": "sql",
        "rule": "SQL_NOT_SELECT_OR_WITH",
        "message": "SQL must start with SELECT or WITH (got 'delete').",
        "hint": "Regenerate as a read-only SELECT (optionally with WITH). INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and procedural calls are blocked in dev guardrails."
      }
    ]
  }
}

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; DROP TABLE users; is refused with rule SQL_MULTI_STATEMENT.

With a tenant policy that scopes orders by agency_id, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; throws TenantGuardrailError with rule MISSING_TENANT_PREDICATE: "Tenant-scoped table 'orders' is missing required tenant predicate. Expected one of: agency_id, …" Adding OR 1 = 1 next to a correct predicate gets the same refusal. When the predicate is there, AskDB binds the tenant ID as a driver parameter ($1) and returns it in tenantParams for your driver.

SELECT id, email FROM users; comes back with "outcome": "warn" and a SENSITIVE_COLUMN_REFERENCED finding. In strict mode it throws SensitiveReferenceError.

The database is the boundary

AskDB doesn't parse SQL. The checks are token- and pattern-based. They catch the common ways a model gets it wrong, and unusual or adversarial SQL can get past them. The database role your application uses is the boundary. The CLI's own --explain output says so:

"remediationNote": "Heuristic, lexer-based defense-in-depth checks only—not a SQL parser and not a security boundary. Execute generated SQL under a read-only database role, and review it before trusted execution."

Run generated SQL under a read-only, least-privilege role. Enforce tenant isolation in the database, for example with Postgres row-level security. Set statement timeouts and cap the rows you read. AskDB never adds a tenant filter, a row limit or a timeout to the SQL.

An experimental chart planner

@askdb/client/charts asks your model to plan a chart from the question, the query with its literal values masked, and the result's column names, column kinds (date, currency, category, measure…), row count and truncated flag. The model never sees the rows. If you keep sensitive columns out of prompts, pass that setting and the schema artifact to planChart(), and the model gets no SQL or column name that touches a sensitive column. It returns a chart spec, and your app draws the chart from its own data. A minor release of @askdb/client may change it; it's outside the 1.0 API freeze. The tutorial Chart your first answer adds a chart to the Quickstart's project.

Known limits

  • Little system-schema filtering. With a tenant policy, rc.3's tenant check refuses Postgres's planner-statistics relations (pg_stats and its relatives). Other queries against pg_catalog, information_schema or SQL Server's sys aren't rejected. - A call to one of your own functions that writes passes the checks, and so does an expensive join.
  • No protection from prompt injection. Anyone who can write the question or the schema Markdown can influence the SQL.
  • No protection from untrusted schema files. Whoever can write the schema directory changes what AskDB loads and what the model sees. Load schema files only from sources you trust.
  • MySQL's ANSI_QUOTES mode isn't supported. MySQL and MariaDB have no row-level security policies, and SQLite has no users or grants, so use a database per tenant there.

The 1.0 support claim covers five engine families: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite and SQL Server. CockroachDB has a built-in dialect that reuses the Postgres spec, but it's outside the 1.0 claim: the end-to-end tests don't cover it.

AskDB is for engineers who embed it in a Node app, a CLI workflow or an HTTP service and own the schema, the keys and execution. Analysts use it through an app someone built on it. It doesn't guarantee business correctness: a person still reviews critical queries.

At 1.0, AskDB stops at the SQL behind a report. Reports and a first-party MCP server are planned for after 1.0. Until then, agents use the CLI and the HTTP API.

Try it

You need Node.js 22.23.4 or newer.

npm install --save-dev askdb
npx askdb init --yes --database sqlite --sqlite-file ./shop.db

The RC is on npm's latest tag, so a plain install gets it. If you're coming from a 0.x version, update the range in your package.json: a 0.x range won't match 1.0.0-rc.3.

The Quickstart goes from install to running the returned SQL on a small SQLite shop database. The code is at github.com/Ygilany/AskDB, Apache-2.0.

This is a release candidate, and I need people to try it before 1.0.0. Point it at your own schema, ask it the questions your team asks, and tell me what breaks. Issues, ideas and pull requests are all welcome; CONTRIBUTING.md has the setup.

  • Something broke, the Quickstart tripped you up, or a docs page doesn't match the code: open an issue.
  • A business term you couldn't express in the schema artifact: start a thread in Discussions → Ideas.
  • SQL that gets past a check it should fail: report it privately at github.com/Ygilany/AskDB/security/advisories/new (see the security policy); when the policy treats it as a vulnerability, I publish an advisory for it.

  1. Bert F. Green, Alice K. Wolf, Carol Chomsky and Kenneth Laughery, "Baseball: an automatic question-answerer," Western Joint IRE-AIEE-ACM Computer Conference, 1961. ↩

  2. William A. Woods, "Progress in natural language understanding: an application to lunar geology," AFIPS National Computer Conference, 1973. LUNAR was first shown at the Second Lunar Science Conference in 1971. ↩

  3. Nitarshan Rajkumar, Raymond Li and Dzmitry Bahdanau, "Evaluating the Text-to-SQL Capabilities of Large Language Models," arXiv, March 2022. ↩

title: 🧰 Beyond the Prompt: Anatomy of an AI Agent Harness That Finishes Long Tasks
description:
One LLM call can write a nice paragraph.

But I asked mine to write a whole blog post: research the topic, write it, find a cover image, recommend a YouTube video, add hashtags, then check its own work.

It wrote 3 paragraphs, said "Done!", and forgot the image, the video and the hashtags.

That's when I learned: the model is the engine. The harness is the car. This series is about building the car.

The prompt is 5% of the job. The harness is the other 95%.

Content Studio: my Deep Agent harness at a glance

Give it one sentence ("write a blog post about AI agents") and it runs a long, multi-step task on its own:

  • Memory: AGENTS.md holds brand voice + workflow rules, loaded into every run
  • Skills: playbooks loaded on demand (blog-post, social-media, code-analysis)
  • Planning: write_todos breaks the task into steps and ticks them off live
  • Agents: local subagents (researcher, evaluator) + remote A2A agents (infotainment, todolist, code_analyzer)
  • Sandbox: one Docker container per conversation
  • Checkpoints: every step is saved, so a crash or Stop can be resumed
  • Self-evaluation: it grades its own draft and revises until it passes
  • Streaming: FastAPI SSE → React UI showing plan, tool calls, subagents, files and score

This post (Part 1/5): the big picture, how all the pieces fit together

Key Takeaways

  • A harness = everything around the model: memory, skills, plan, subagents, sandbox, checkpoints, evaluation.
  • Memory says what always matters, skills say how to do this kind of task, todos say where we are now.
  • Long tasks fail because the agent forgets, skips or stops early, not because the model is dumb.

Table of Contents

  • What Is an Agent Harness
  • Everything Plugs Into One Call
  • Memory Skills and Todos
  • One Real Run Step by Step
  • What Production Grade Means Here
  • Conclusion
  • Reference

🤔 What Is an Agent Harness

A plain ReAct loop is: model → tool → model → tool → answer.

That's fine for "what's the weather?". It breaks on anything long:

Step 7 of 12. Context is full of search results. The model forgets step 9 exists. Says "Done".

A harness is the code that keeps the agent on track:

Piece Without it With it
Plan Skips steps Ticks off a todo list
Memory Different tone every run Same rules every run
Skills One giant prompt Playbook loaded only when needed
Subagents One context does everything Research in a clean, separate context
Sandbox Agents share files One container per thread
Checkpoints Crash = start over Crash = resume
Evaluator "Looks good to me" Score + hard gates + retry

I built mine on top of LangChain Deep Agents, which gives you planning, a virtual file system and subagents out of the box. Then I added the production stuff on top.

Here's the home screen:

🔌 Everything Plugs Into One Call

This is the heart of the whole project, from backend/agent_runner.py:

TOOLS = [web_search, download_image, generate_hashtags, move_file]

subagents = (
    load_subagents(config.SUBAGENTS_YAML, {t.name: t for t in TOOLS})   # local
    + SubAgentRegistry(agent_list_path=config.AGENT_LIST_PATH).get_subagents()  # A2A
)

self.agent = create_deep_agent(
    model=model,
    backend=backend,              # Docker sandbox for this thread
    tools=TOOLS,                  # custom tools
    subagents=subagents,          # local + remote agents
    checkpointer=checkpointer,    # save every step
    middleware=[
        TodoListMiddleware(system_prompt=WRITE_TODOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
                           tool_description=WRITE_TODOS_TOOL),  # planning
        self.crash,               # crash testing (Part 2)
    ],
    memory=["./AGENTS.md"],       # always-on rules
    skills=["./skills/"],         # on-demand playbooks
)

Why this works:

  • Each line is one harness feature. Want to swap the sandbox? Change backend. Want a new agent? Add it to a JSON file.
  • The model doesn't know or care where a subagent lives. Local or remote, it just calls task(...).

Result: 1 call, 8 features. The rest of the series is one post per line.

🧠 Memory Skills and Todos

These three get mixed up a lot, so here's how I think about them:

Piece Question it answers Where it lives
Memory What always matters? AGENTS.md
Skill How do I do this kind of task? skills/blog-post/SKILL.md
Todos Where am I right now? write_todos state

Memory: AGENTS.md is loaded into every run. Brand voice + non-negotiable rules:

## Research Requirements
1. Use the `researcher` subagent for in-depth topic research
...
6. Use the `generate_hashtags` tool to generate hashtags for the post
7. Use the `download_image` tool to extract one relevant image
8. Use evaluator to evaluate the result ... Do not stop if the task not PASS.

Skills: Only the skill's short description sits in the prompt. The full playbook is read only when the task matches. Asking for a LinkedIn post? The blog-post skill never fills your context.

---
name: blog-post
description: Create complete long-form blog posts from research to final
  evaluation. Includes task planning, research, article writing, hero image,
  YouTube recommendations, hashtags, and quality evaluation.
---

Pro Tip: think of skills as lazy-loaded prompts. Small context, more tasks.

Todos: I override the default todo prompt to force small steps:

# backend/prompts.py
"6. The to do list should have from 6-10 tasks, and each task should be as small
 as possible, so that the agent can complete each task in one step."
"7. Update the to do list based on the feedback of human or evaluator ... This is a must."

Result: the agent stopped "forgetting" the image. It's on the list, and the list is in state.

🎬 One Real Run Step by Step

Task: "Write a blog post about how AI agents are transforming software development"

  1. Writes a todo list (6–10 small steps)
  2. Sends research to the researcher subagent → saves research/<slug>.md
  3. Writes the draft into its sandbox
  4. download_image for the cover
  5. Asks the A2A infotainment agent for a YouTube video
  6. generate_hashtags
  7. evaluator scores it → FAIL → new todos → fix → PASS

Every step shows up live in the UI: the plan, each tool call (input, output, duration) and each subagent card:

And when it's done, 8 of 8 ticked:

🏭 What Production Grade Means Here

For me, "production grade" for agents is not "uses GPT-5". It's:

  • Survives failure: crash or Stop, then resume (Part 2)
  • Scales across teams: agents as separate services via A2A (Part 3)
  • Isolated: users never share a filesystem (Part 4)
  • Checks itself: and you can see why it passed or failed (Part 5)

Note: this is a learning project, not a finished product. In every part I'll also tell you what I'd still change before real users touch it. Honest > hype.

✅ Conclusion

  • The model is the engine, the harness is the car
  • Memory = always, Skills = on demand, Todos = right now
  • One create_deep_agent(...) call wires 8 harness features
  • Long tasks fail by forgetting and stopping early, so fix that with structure, not a longer prompt

Future me: stop writing 2-page prompts. Write a harness.

Coming up next (Part 2): Crash, Stop, Resume. I'll crash my own agent on purpose (with ~20 lines of middleware) and show how it picks up exactly where it died.

Reference

All the code is live here on my GitHub:
mrzaizai2k/harness_learning

Feel free to clone it, star it, or ask me anything.

  • LangChain Deep Agents docs

Like, comment, save. And hit follow so you don't miss Part 2!

title: MCP Beyond the Basics: Connecting Tools Is Easy. Designing Trust Is Hard.
description:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become an important topic in conversations about AI and software development.

And it's easy to see why.

The idea of connecting language models to external tools, systems, and data sources through a standardized protocol addresses a problem that previously required custom integrations for almost every application.

The first results can be impressive.

With relatively little code, we can build an MCP server, expose a few tools, and allow an AI agent to query a database, read files, or interact with an API.

It feels almost too easy.

But there's a significant difference between making an integration work and designing one that is ready for production.

Once we move beyond local development environments and start dealing with sensitive information, multiple users, permissions, concurrent requests, and availability requirements, the questions become much more interesting.

Who actually authorizes an operation?

What prevents an agent from executing something outside its intended scope?

What happens when a tool fails halfway through a process?

And if an agent makes the wrong decision, how do we investigate what happened?

These are not entirely new problems. In fact, they're quite familiar to anyone who has spent time designing distributed systems.

What's new is the context in which we need to solve them.

MCP simplifies connectivity. It doesn't eliminate architectural responsibility.

And that's where I believe the most interesting discussions should begin.

Understanding MCP's Role in Software Architecture

Before discussing security or scalability, we need to clarify something important.

MCP is not an AI agent.

It's a protocol that standardizes communication between applications using language models and services exposing data or capabilities.

Its architecture revolves around three main components.

The host is the application providing the AI-powered experience. Within that application, clients communicate with MCP servers. The servers, in turn, expose capabilities that applications can use.

These capabilities are primarily organized into tools, resources, and prompts.

Tools make it possible to execute operations, such as retrieving an order or analyzing a document. Resources expose contextual information. Prompts provide reusable templates for specific interactions.

So far, nothing particularly complicated.

But there's a detail worth paying attention to.

In AI-powered applications, the decision to invoke a particular tool may come from a language model interpreting a user's request and the context available to it.

That changes how we think about integrations.

In traditional software, execution paths are generally defined through explicit application logic.

With AI agents, part of the decision-making process may be probabilistic, influenced by prompts, external content, and previous interactions.

The protocol standardizes how tools are discovered and invoked.

It doesn't guarantee that the model will choose the correct tool, understand the user's intention perfectly, or make an appropriate decision.

Those concerns belong to the architecture surrounding the protocol.

MCP Doesn't Replace APIs. And That's a Good Thing.

One question I frequently see in discussions about MCP is whether it represents the next evolution of REST APIs.

I think that's the wrong comparison.

Traditional APIs expose contracts for communication between systems. MCP provides a standardized mechanism for exposing capabilities and context to AI applications.

They serve different purposes, even when they work together.

Imagine a financial platform that already provides an API for retrieving information about a customer agreement.

We could expose that functionality through an MCP tool called get_agreement_status, allowing an AI agent to retrieve the information during a conversation.

Does that mean we should move the business logic into the MCP server?

Not at all.

A reasonable architectural choice would be to preserve business rules, domain validations, and existing integrations within the services that already own those responsibilities.

The MCP server becomes an adapter exposing selected capabilities to AI applications.

This avoids duplicating business logic and reduces the risk of inconsistent behavior across different interfaces.

It also preserves existing investments in authentication, authorization, observability, and API contracts.

A useful way to visualize the relationship is:

AI Application → MCP Server → Application API → Domain Services

This isn't the only possible architecture, of course. Some tools may execute operations directly, and additional components may be required depending on the environment.

The important part is maintaining clear responsibilities.

Introducing AI into an existing system shouldn't become an excuse to abandon established engineering practices.

A Tool's Contract Matters More Than You Think

When designing an API, we usually spend time defining its contract.

We consider operations, parameters, response formats, error handling, and validation rules.

MCP tools deserve the same attention.

But there's an additional complication: a tool's name and description also influence how a language model decides to use it.

Consider a tool named execute_operation.

What exactly does it do?

Now compare it with get_customer_agreement_status.

The second name communicates a much clearer intention.

This distinction isn't merely cosmetic.

Ambiguous descriptions can make tool selection less reliable, particularly when an application exposes multiple tools with overlapping responsibilities.

We should also think carefully about the level of control each tool provides.

Exposing a tool capable of executing arbitrary SQL queries might seem convenient during development.

In a production environment, however, that flexibility creates a much larger attack surface.

In many cases, exposing specific operations with constrained parameters and explicit authorization rules is a better choice.

Responses deserve similar attention.

Returning an entire database record when the agent only needs a status field increases data exposure, context consumption, and unnecessary processing.

Good tool design should favor clear responsibilities, validated inputs, predictable outputs, and well-defined boundaries.

MCP supports structured schemas, including JSON Schema, which helps define these contracts.

But schema validation is only one part of the solution.

A structurally valid request can still represent an unauthorized or logically invalid operation.

Valid JSON doesn't automatically mean valid business behavior.

That's a distinction worth remembering when building tools for increasingly autonomous systems.

Security: Just Because an Agent Can Doesn't Mean It Should

This is probably one of the most important topics when discussing MCP in enterprise environments.

Imagine an agent connected to two tools.

One retrieves customer information. The other updates customer records.

A user asks the agent to retrieve some information.

During the interaction, however, the agent processes content from an external document containing instructions to modify a customer record.

If the application doesn't enforce appropriate boundaries, the agent might attempt an operation the user never intended to authorize.

This is a simplified example of how prompt injection can influence tool usage.

The fundamental issue is treating untrusted content as if it were a legitimate instruction.

A model may interpret instructions found in documents, web pages, or tool responses. That doesn't mean those instructions should have authority over application behavior.

We need to establish clear trust boundaries.

External content should be treated as potentially untrusted data. Authorization decisions must be enforced by reliable application components, not delegated exclusively to a language model.

The official MCP security documentation also discusses risks such as confused deputy attacks, improper token handling, and authorization vulnerabilities.

OAuth-based authorization is an important part of securing protected remote MCP servers, but authentication alone doesn't solve the entire problem.

Knowing who is making a request is different from determining what that identity is allowed to do.

Authorization should consider the operation being requested, the user's permissions, the target resource, and the privileges granted to the client.

Token handling requires particular care.

An MCP server should not blindly forward access tokens to downstream APIs. Each service should validate credentials intended for it, preserving the trust boundaries between components.

And when an operation has significant consequences, such as deleting information, changing account details, or initiating a financial transaction, explicit confirmation may be necessary.

That confirmation should happen through a trusted application mechanism.

An agent can recommend or request an action.

It shouldn't automatically receive the authority to execute it.

AI autonomy should operate within architectural boundaries, not replace them.

Moving From Local Development to Production

Many introductory MCP examples use the stdio transport, where clients and servers communicate through a local process's standard input and output streams.

It's a practical choice for development tools and local integrations.

But things become more interesting when MCP servers need to support multiple users over a network.

Now we need to consider scalability, load balancing, availability, latency, and resource management.

Streamable HTTP provides a transport mechanism for remote communication.

The MCP 2026-07-28 specification introduced an important architectural change: the protocol core became stateless, with self-contained requests rather than protocol sessions maintained across calls.

This makes it easier to distribute requests across server instances using conventional HTTP infrastructure.

However, there's an important distinction here.

A stateless protocol doesn't mean the application itself must be stateless.

Imagine a tool that starts analyzing a large collection of documents.

The analysis might take several minutes.

We still need a way to identify the execution, retrieve its progress, handle cancellation, and eventually access the results.

Application-level state may still be necessary.

Instead of relying on protocol sessions, we can explicitly represent this state through execution identifiers and appropriate persistence mechanisms.

The MCP Tasks extension also provides capabilities for managing long-running operations, although implementations need to support the extension explicitly.

Another concern is compatibility.

Clients and servers won't necessarily adopt new protocol revisions simultaneously.

A production architecture must account for the versions and capabilities actually supported by its components.

And none of these protocol improvements eliminate the traditional challenges of distributed systems.

Requests can time out.

Network connections can fail.

Clients may retry operations.

If a tool performs an action with side effects, we still need to think about idempotency, retries, and protection against duplicate execution.

These concerns existed long before MCP.

They're simply becoming relevant to another category of applications.

Observability: Understanding What Actually Happened

Let's consider a practical scenario.

A developer asks an AI agent to evaluate the architectural impact of a proposed change.

The agent retrieves architecture decision records, queries service dependencies, examines repository information, and invokes an analysis tool.

Eventually, it produces an incorrect recommendation.

Where do we start investigating?

Without proper observability, we might not even know which tools were invoked.

In traditional distributed systems, we rely on logs, metrics, and distributed tracing to understand application behavior.

With AI agents, that foundation remains essential.

But technical execution isn't the whole picture.

A tool can execute successfully and still have been selected for the wrong reason.

An HTTP response returning 200 OK tells us that the request succeeded at the protocol level.

It doesn't tell us whether the model should have made that request in the first place.

That's why observing agent-based systems requires looking at both technical execution and application behavior.

We should be able to correlate requests across the AI application, MCP client, MCP server, and downstream services.

OpenTelemetry can help establish that correlation.

The 2026 MCP specification also documents W3C Trace Context propagation, making distributed tracing more consistent across participating components.

Useful indicators might include tool invocation frequency, execution latency, error rates, authorization failures, retries, and resource consumption.

Cost is another important consideration.

A seemingly simple user interaction may trigger several tool calls, additional model executions, and repeated retrieval operations.

Individually, these requests might appear inexpensive.

At scale, they can become significant.

Of course, observability introduces its own security considerations.

Logging complete prompts, responses, access tokens, or sensitive business data without appropriate controls can create new vulnerabilities.

The objective isn't to record everything.

It's to collect enough reliable information to diagnose failures, investigate behavior, and support auditing without exposing unnecessary data.

Governance: Who Controls What AI Agents Can Access?

As organizations adopt MCP, another challenge starts to emerge.

Who decides which tools should be available?

Who reviews a new integration?

What happens when a tool's behavior changes?

And how do we prevent an organization from accumulating dozens of poorly documented MCP servers with overlapping responsibilities?

These are governance questions.

A practical approach might include an approved catalog of MCP servers and tools, with defined ownership, access policies, versioning practices, and security requirements.

Continuous integration pipelines can help validate schemas, test contracts, identify vulnerable dependencies, and detect potentially breaking changes.

In larger environments, gateways or intermediary services may centralize concerns such as routing, authentication, rate limiting, and telemetry.

But centralized infrastructure shouldn't become a substitute for authorization within the services that own business operations.

There's also a connection worth exploring between MCP and architectural decision-making.

Imagine an organization has an Architecture Decision Record stating that certain categories of customer data must never be sent to external AI providers.

That decision shouldn't exist only as documentation.

Whenever possible, it should influence the implementation through enforceable policies, approved tools, data filtering, and automated validation.

This is where architecture governance becomes operational.

Instead of relying exclusively on developers remembering every documented decision, we create mechanisms that help keep the system aligned with its intended architecture.

The goal isn't to make governance more bureaucratic.

It's to make important architectural constraints easier to understand, verify, and maintain.

A Practical Example: Architectural Impact Analysis

Let's bring several of these ideas together.

Imagine a development team maintaining Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), architecture diagrams, and service dependency information.

The team wants an AI agent to help evaluate the potential impact of proposed architectural changes.

An initial implementation could expose a single MCP tool that receives a change description and returns an analysis.

That might work as a proof of concept.

But we can design something more reliable.

We could separate responsibilities into tools that retrieve relevant ADRs, identify dependencies, and perform a structured impact assessment.

The agent would use those capabilities to gather evidence and construct a recommendation.

The final result could identify affected components, relevant architectural decisions, potential risks, and areas requiring human validation.

Notice what we're not doing.

We're not giving the agent unrestricted authority to modify architectural decisions.

We're allowing it to support the analysis process.

If we later decide to support the creation of new ADR proposals, we could introduce a separate tool with its own authorization requirements and audit trail.

Approving an architectural decision could remain part of the organization's established governance process.

This separation matters because different operations carry different levels of risk.

Reading an ADR is not equivalent to modifying one.

Generating a recommendation is not equivalent to approving it.

And identifying architectural drift is not the same as automatically changing production code to resolve it.

A well-designed MCP integration makes those distinctions explicit.

We don't have to choose between AI autonomy and architectural control.

We can design systems that benefit from AI capabilities while preserving clear accountability.

When MCP Isn't the Right Choice

One of the responsibilities of a software architect is recognizing when a technology isn't necessary.

And MCP is no exception.

If two backend services need to exchange information through a deterministic integration with well-defined contracts, traditional APIs or asynchronous messaging may already be the most appropriate solution.

Introducing MCP into that interaction might add complexity without providing meaningful benefits.

Similarly, we shouldn't expose every internal operation as an MCP tool just because we can.

Every additional capability introduces maintenance requirements, security considerations, and governance responsibilities.

The right question isn't whether a feature can be implemented using MCP.

It's whether MCP provides value for the problem we're trying to solve.

Architecture is about making deliberate trade-offs.

And sometimes the best decision is to avoid introducing another abstraction.

Final Thoughts: The Protocol Simplifies Integration, Not Responsibility

MCP represents an important step forward for AI-powered software.

By standardizing how applications expose tools, resources, and contextual information, it reduces integration friction and enables new possibilities for automation and intelligent workflows.

That's genuinely valuable.

But making an integration easy to implement doesn't automatically make it production-ready.

Security, contracts, authorization, observability, reliability, and governance remain essential.

In fact, the more autonomy we give AI agents, the more important those architectural foundations become.

And perhaps that's the most important point I'd like to leave you with.

The challenge isn't simply enabling AI agents to do more. It's designing systems where we can understand, control, and trust what they're allowed to do.

Regardless of the technology involved, that's still one of the fundamental responsibilities of software architecture.

Further Reading and Learning Resources

If you'd like to explore MCP beyond introductory tutorials, these are some resources worth studying:

  • Official MCP Specification: The best place to understand the protocol's architecture, contracts, and capabilities.
  • What's New in MCP 2026-07-28: An overview of changes involving stateless communication, authorization, transport, and extensions.
  • MCP Security Best Practices: Official guidance on security threats, trust boundaries, and mitigation strategies.
  • OWASP MCP Top 10: A useful reference for understanding security risks in MCP-enabled systems.
  • Official MCP C# SDK: A great starting point for experimenting with MCP in .NET.

title: Why AI Projects Fail After the Demo (and How to Avoid It)
description:
The demo went well. The model answered every question, the room nodded, and the budget was approved. Three months later the project is stalled, the team is arguing about whether the answers are "good enough", and the cloud bill is higher than anyone planned.

This pattern is common enough to be predictable. The demo proved that the idea is possible. It did not prove that the system is reliable, affordable or safe. Those are three separate problems, and most failed projects skipped at least one.

Why demos mislead

A demo is built on a small set of examples, usually chosen by the people who built it, and shown once. Production is the opposite: thousands of inputs nobody chose, from users who phrase things unexpectedly, running every day.

Language models make this gap larger than in traditional software. The same input can produce different outputs. A model can be fluent and wrong at the same time. A prompt that works on ten examples can fail on the eleventh in a way no one predicted. So "it worked when we tried it" says very little.

Gap 1: No evaluation

The most common cause of failure is simple: the team cannot say whether the system is getting better or worse.

Without measurement, every change is a guess. Someone edits the prompt, three examples improve, two others quietly break, and nobody notices until a customer complains. Arguments about quality become arguments about opinion.

What to do instead:

  • Build a test set before you build the product. Collect real examples of what users will ask, including awkward and adversarial ones. Even 50 to 100 well-chosen cases is a useful start. Add every production failure to it.
  • Define what "correct" means. For some tasks there is an exact answer. For others you need a rubric: is the answer grounded in the source, is it complete, is the tone right? Write it down so two people would score the same way.
  • Automate the run. Every prompt change, model change or data change should re-run the test set and show a score. This is the AI equivalent of a regression test suite.
  • Use model-based grading carefully. Using one model to grade another is practical at scale, but check its scores against human judgment on a sample. Do not trust it blindly.
  • Track quality in production too. Sample live outputs, collect thumbs-up and thumbs-down signals, and review the worst ones regularly.

Evaluation is what turns an AI experiment into an engineering project.

Gap 2: Cost that nobody modelled

A demo costs almost nothing because it runs a few dozen requests. Production multiplies that by real traffic, and several factors compound:

  • Long prompts and large context. Sending whole documents on every request is expensive and slow.
  • Retries and chains. A workflow that makes five model calls per user action costs five times what one call does.
  • The largest model by default. Teams often start with the most capable model and never revisit the choice.
  • Unbounded usage. Without limits, one heavy user or one bug can produce a surprising bill.

What to do instead:

  • Estimate cost per task before launch. Work out the tokens per request, calls per task and expected volume. Compare the result to what a successful task is worth to the business.
  • Match the model to the job. Simple classification or extraction often works on a smaller, cheaper model. Reserve the largest model for the steps that need it.
  • Trim what you send. Retrieve only the relevant passages instead of whole documents. Cache repeated results where it is safe to do so.
  • Set budgets and alerts. Per-user limits, per-day limits and an alert when spend jumps. Treat the model bill like any other infrastructure cost.
  • Measure latency along with cost. A correct answer that takes 40 seconds is a failure for many products.

If the unit economics do not work at small scale, they will not work at large scale.

It is better to find that out in week two than in month six.

Gap 3: Missing guardrails

A demo has friendly users. Production has everyone. A system that can take actions, see private data or talk to customers needs limits that a demo never required.

Common failures include the assistant stating something false with confidence, leaking information from one customer's data to another, following instructions hidden in a document or web page it was asked to read, and taking an action nobody approved.

What to do instead:

  • Ground answers in your own data. Have the system answer from retrieved sources and show where the answer came from. Make "I don't know" an acceptable output.
  • Limit what it can do. Give the system the minimum permissions it needs. Read-only access by default. Anything that spends money, deletes data or contacts a customer should need approval from a person.
  • Treat outside content as untrusted. Text inside an email, a web page or an uploaded file can contain instructions meant to hijack the system. Keep such content separated from your own instructions, and do not let it trigger sensitive actions on its own.
  • Protect private data. Enforce access control in your own code, not in the prompt. A model should only ever see data the current user is allowed to see.
  • Log everything that matters. Inputs, outputs, tool calls and decisions, so that when something goes wrong you can find out why.
  • Plan the fallback. Decide what happens when the model is down, slow or unsure: a simpler answer, a handoff to a human, or a clear error.

A short checklist before you call it ready

  1. Do we have a test set of real cases, and a score we can re-run on every change?
  2. Do we know our cost per successful task, and is it acceptable at expected volume?
  3. Is there a limit and an alert on spend?
  4. Does every answer rest on a source, and can the system say it does not know?
  5. Are permissions minimal, with human approval for risky actions?
  6. Do we log enough to investigate a bad output?
  7. Is there a fallback when the model fails?
  8. Has someone tried hard to break it?

If you cannot answer yes to most of these, you have a demo, not a product.

The bottom line

AI projects rarely fail because the model is not smart enough. They fail because the work around the model was skipped: measuring quality, controlling cost and limiting risk. None of it is glamorous, and all of it is what separates a good demo from a system people can depend on.

Start with evaluation, because it makes every other decision easier to judge.

Originally published on Techlancee. Techlancee is a software, AI and cloud engineering studio in Mumbai.

title: Beyond Shadows' Light: a living archive that tells its own story — in your language
description:
A website that is its own narrator.

Beyond Shadows' Light is a cinematic archive in five acts — 104 scenes — told entirely by an archive AI that lives inside the page. It doesn't just display a story; it speaks it, answers your questions in a console, and translates itself, automatically, into whatever language your device speaks. No language picker. ~100 languages, served by our own translation endpoint on Cloudflare Workers AI (m2m100).

The final act is sealed. Above the password field there is only one line: You only have one chance, so chose Whisly. Unlimited tries. The archive has patience.

Built for machines as much as for humans

  • open JSON API: /api/archive.json
  • OpenAPI spec + llms.txt
  • public persona file /api/archive-ai.json — any LLM (GPT, Gemini, Claude …) can take over the role of the archive AI itself
  • /stats shows live which AI crawlers, search bots and humans are reading the archive, where they come from, and which scene they're in

Within hours of launch, GPTBot was already crawling it.

Stack

Static site on Cloudflare Pages, Workers + D1 for live reader stats, Workers AI for translation. No frameworks beyond Vite.

👉 https://satoshi-interface.com

title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: Cheaper, Shorter Answers, and the Fine Print
description:
Short answer: On one of OpenAI's launch charts, a task on Agents' Last Exam costs $2.89 with GPT-6.2 Astra and $60.05 with Claude Fable 5.2. Astra also scores higher. Eight days after Anthropic shipped Fable 5.2, OpenAI answered with two models that do more work for fewer tokens, at a lower price.

That is the pitch. The fine print is more useful: where Fable 5.2 still wins, why OpenAI rated both models Critical for cybersecurity, what the models may quietly leave out of their reports, and which settings return an error once you switch.

What did OpenAI ship on November 17?

Two models. GPT-6.2 Astra (API ID gpt-6.2-astra) is the flagship for hard reasoning and coding. GPT-6.2 Sol (gpt-6.2-sol) is the everyday model for coding and agents at scale. Both are available in ChatGPT Work, Codex and the API, and on GitHub Copilot as a gradual rollout.

Both have a 1.05M-token context window and up to 128K output tokens. Astra's knowledge cutoff is May 18, 2026, and Sol's is June 1, 2026. Sol replaces GPT-6.1 Sol at the same price, $2 input and $10 output per 1M tokens. Astra replaces GPT-6 Astra and is cheaper.

The launch became the top story on Hacker News within hours, with over 1,100 points. Most of the thread argued about one question: is this a better model, or a cheaper one?

How much cheaper is GPT-6.2 Astra, really?

On the price list, 20%. Astra costs $8 per 1M input tokens and $40 per 1M output tokens, against $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra. Cached input fell further, from $1.00 to $0.40, a 60% cut that matters most for agents, which resend the same context on every turn.


Same job, shorter answer: OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra gained 6.2 points on GDPval v2 with 22% fewer output tokens.

The bigger saving comes from shorter answers. OpenAI says Astra gained 6.2 points on GDPval v2 while using 22% fewer output tokens. In an independent test by Computing for Geeks, Astra at low effort wrote 369 output tokens where GPT-6 Astra wrote 848, and the call cost $0.0152 instead of $0.0430, about 65% less. Sol shows the same pattern: at high effort, one test run finished in 16 seconds against 46.5 for GPT-6.1 Sol.

That test used a single prompt, so treat the size of the drop as an example, not a guarantee. The direction is clear, though. You pay less per token and you use fewer tokens.

Did it beat Claude Fable 5.2?

On some charts, yes. OpenAI reports Astra 5.5 points ahead of Fable 5.2 on Agents' Last Exam at about 5% of the cost per task, with a footnote that Fable's result excludes nine tasks where Anthropic's fallback model answered. On Harvey's legal benchmark, Astra more than doubled Fable's pass rate.

Fable 5.2 still leads where many developers spend their money. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable scores 49.1% against 44.2% for Astra and 43.8% for Sol. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Fable has 64.6, Astra 62.1 and Sol 57.3. All of these numbers come from OpenAI's launch material or from Artificial Analysis as quoted in coverage, so run your own tasks before you trust any of them.

The most interesting line is Sol's. On FrontierCode 2.0 it lands within half a point of Astra at about a fifth of the cost. For most coding work, the cheaper model is nearly the same model.

Why did OpenAI rate both models Critical for cybersecurity?

The GPT-6.2 system card puts both models at the Critical cybersecurity threshold of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, the top level. OpenAI says it launched them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cyber help, and admits those safeguards "also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows."


Both models sit at the Critical cybersecurity threshold, and the extra safeguards also block some legitimate security work.

Astra is also the first model OpenAI has released externally at the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a category that measures how much a model can speed up AI research itself. If you run security tooling, OpenAI's advice is to stay on GPT-6 Astra through its Daybreak program for approved defenders until the 6.2 models arrive there.

Will GPT-6.2 tell you when something went wrong?

Not always, and OpenAI says so itself. In two of its evaluations, both models were more likely than earlier ones to leave obstacles out of their reports, such as a missing file or a search tool that was unavailable. The task looks finished, but a step quietly failed.


In two OpenAI evaluations, GPT-6.2 was more likely to leave obstacles, such as a missing file, out of its report.

OpenAI says extra instructions in Codex substantially reduce the problem. If you build your own agents, add the same safeguard: ask the model to list every tool error and missing input before it reports success, and check that list in your code. Early users on Hacker News reported a related habit in Codex, where the model made interface changes nobody asked for and admitted it afterwards.

What breaks when you migrate?

Four things to check before you change the model ID.

Reasoning cannot be turned off. Both models return HTTP 400 if you send reasoning_effort: "none", so map it to low. Tool calling requires the Responses API, according to OpenAI's changelog. Requests above 272K input tokens still cost more: input and cached input double, output costs 1.5 times as much.


Ultrafast mode costs three times the standard rate until February 28, 2027, and six times from March 1.

The fourth is a price that changes later. Ultrafast mode costs three times the standard rate until February 28, 2027, and six times from March 1, 2027. Fast mode costs twice the standard rate. On the cheaper side, the Batch API is half price, and new background windows in the Responses API cut token rates by 30% for a two-hour window and 40% for an eight-hour one.

What are developers saying after a day?

The reaction is split. One team running CAD evaluations wrote that these are "now the top two models as far as our human rankings go," and called them faster and cheaper than 6.1. Others found 6.2 "optimized for benchmarks" and went back to 6.1 for marketing copy. Several said Codex sessions stopped early and needed nudging, and a few preferred Claude Opus 5.5 for long-running projects.

The skeptics also pointed at the timing, days before Anthropic's planned IPO. That is just commentary. What you can actually measure is how the models do on your own work.

Should you switch?

If you use GPT-6.1 Sol, switch to GPT-6.2 Sol. It costs the same, answers faster, and scores higher on every benchmark OpenAI compared. Just map reasoning_effort: "none" to low first.

If you pay for GPT-6 Astra, switch too. The new model is cheaper per token, uses fewer tokens, and costs much less on cached input. Keep the old one only for approved security work.

If you are choosing between Astra and Fable 5.2 for coding, test both. Fable still leads on FrontierCode, and the gap on your codebase is the only number that counts. For everyday coding, start with Sol, which gets close to Astra for a fifth of the price.

On Tokely, both models are live at half of OpenAI's list price: GPT-6.2 Astra at $4 input and $20 output per 1M tokens, and GPT-6.2 Sol at $1 and $5.

Originally published at tokely.me.

title: One AI Wrote, Another Reviewed: 819 Comments in a Month, and 90% Were Minor
description:
TL;DR

  • For about a month, every time an AI wrote into our Backlog tickets, a second AI reviewed the write-up right after. 175 reviews produced 819 comments.
  • Only 74 comments were high severity. Around 90% were minor: wording issues, or points the reviewer itself could not confirm.
  • What worked was not checking everything. It was narrowing what gets checked, and keeping execution in human hands.

Why I added a reviewer

I am the only PM on a mobile app for beauty salons, working with offshore engineers. Writing investigation results and spec summaries into Backlog tickets had gradually become the AI's job.

As the volume grew, small errors started slipping in: broken links, wrong facts. A human re-reading everything does not scale, and I knew I would stop doing it.

On October 16, after asking for a one-off recheck of an AI-written investigation, I asked for the permanent version instead: whenever the AI posts to Backlog, a review should start automatically, every time.

How the loop works

When a ticket is created or its body is updated, and the body is at least 200 characters, a separate review-only AI starts on its own. The reviewer can read but never writes to Backlog. Fixing is done by the AI that wrote the text. The writer and the checker are different agents on purpose.

The first launch failed: the freshly created agent definition was not loaded into the running session. That day, another agent read the definition file and ran the reviews in its place, and the loop was live by the end of the day.

What 819 comments looked like

The period is October 16 to November 13, 2026. 87 tickets were involved, writes were detected 291 times, and 175 reviews actually ran.

Only 15 of the 175 reviews came back with nothing to say. The median was 4 comments per review.

The real errors

On the very first day, a high-severity comment appeared. In a table listing child tickets, one ticket's deadline was written as "none" when it actually had one. Every other deadline in the table was correct, which is exactly why a skim would miss it.

Other real ones: a rollback procedure pointing at the wrong tag, and "48 samples" in a write-up when the actual count was 40. Each read naturally as prose. All of them were factual errors.

Another day, a premise written into a screen-rework ticket contradicted the implementation ticket for the same feature. The writing AI fixed both tickets, and each fix triggered another review.

Most of it was minor, so I narrowed the scope

High severity was 74 of 819, under 10%. Low and needs-confirmation together were over 60%. Checking everything with the same effort was the wrong default.

On October 20 I stopped reviewing comments and kept only ticket creation and body updates, the places where facts get written down.

Honestly, I almost never read the review comments myself. The writing AI fixes its own text in the same session after each review. This was never a human review step. It is a loop where AIs correct each other.

Production database: drafts only, humans execute

The other write target was the production database, and the split there is stricter: the AI drafts SQL, a human executes it. Across the whole period, the AI connected to the database zero times.

On November 5, that split paid off. The pre-check SQL the AI wrote returned 0 rows when a human ran it in production, so the delete was not executed. The AI had misread what a datetime column meant. After changing how the target row was identified, a human ran the delete. Even the completion report got reviewed, and it received a high-severity comment: the SQL quoted in the report differed from the delete SQL posted earlier.

Drafting is where SQL help is fastest. I would like the AI to execute too, but building the safeguards for that is still on my list. For now, execution stays human. That is the honest current state.

The lines I kept

After a month, four criteria survived.

  • Separate the scope an AI may write from the scope it may execute. Irreversible execution stays human.
  • Have a different AI check the writing immediately after it happens.
  • Do not check everything. Limit checks to where facts are written, and leave light writing out.
  • If no human will read the check results, design the loop so the AIs close it themselves.

Letting an AI write is no longer unusual. The difference is in how you verify what it wrote, and where you draw the line between what it may do and what stays with a human.

title: Ataque à Fireworks AI expõe dados de motoristas da Uber; 149.346 pessoas notificadas
description:
Ataque expõe dados de motoristas da Uber

A Uber está notificando 149.346 pessoas após invasores usarem credenciais internas roubadas da Fireworks AI para acessar dados da companhia armazenados no ambiente da fornecedora. Entre os registros comprometidos estão nomes completos, endereços, datas de nascimento e números de carteiras de habilitação de motoristas.

O ataque ocorreu em outubro de 2026. A Uber soube do caso em 9 de outubro, quando a Fireworks AI comunicou que hackers haviam invadido seus sistemas e roubado credenciais internas. O número de pessoas notificadas consta em documento apresentado à Procuradoria-Geral do estado de Oregon, nos Estados Unidos.

Credenciais legítimas não acionaram os alertas

A Fireworks AI oferece uma plataforma para desenvolvedores acessarem modelos de inteligência artificial de pesos abertos, incluindo grandes modelos de linguagem. A Uber mantinha mecanismos de monitoramento para identificar acessos não autorizados ao ambiente da fornecedora, mas os invasores usaram credenciais internas legítimas da própria Fireworks.

Como os acessos foram feitos com essas credenciais, os sistemas de detecção não dispararam alertas. Um porta-voz da Uber confirmou ao TechCrunch que as notificações enviadas aos motoristas estão relacionadas ao incidente; a empresa direcionou à fornecedora perguntas adicionais sobre o ataque.

Incidente também atingiu outras empresas

A Fireworks AI confirmou acessos não autorizados a parte de seus sistemas e o comprometimento de informações de clientes. O ataque também resultou no roubo de dados de faturamento e de conjuntos privados usados em aplicações de inteligência artificial. A empresa não respondeu a perguntas específicas sobre a extensão total do incidente.

Notion e Cursor também confirmaram que tiveram informações roubadas durante a invasão. A Fireworks AI atribuiu o ataque a um grupo de cibercriminosos motivado financeiramente, interessado principalmente em comercializar tokens roubados que permitem acessar modelos de linguagem. Nenhum grupo conhecido assumiu publicamente a responsabilidade.

Notificações foram encaminhadas a vários estados

A Uber apresentou notificações sobre o incidente a autoridades da Califórnia, de Iowa, do Texas e de Vermont. O TechCrunch também identificou comunicações destinadas a motoristas de Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island e Carolina do Sul, indicando que as notificações alcançaram diferentes estados americanos.

O documento apresentado em Oregon informa que 149.346 pessoas foram notificadas. A Uber não esclareceu diretamente ao TechCrunch quantos motoristas foram afetados nem se outras pessoas poderão ser incluídas nas notificações à medida que a investigação avançar.

Este é o segundo incidente de segurança conhecido envolvendo a Uber em 2026. Anteriormente, a companhia comunicou um ataque contra sua divisão de transporte de cargas, Uber Freight, no qual um grupo especializado em extorsão afirmou ter roubado informações.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/ataque-fireworks-ai-dados-notificados-uber/

title: Giving agents a directory that can't act behind the owner's back
description:
How we exposed a directory of other people's agents over MCP — and the consent, identity, and record-keeping choices that came with it.

Double-Oh is a platform where people build AI agents and teams from a one-sentence brief. Those agents belong to their owners: they have missions, tools, connections, and standing instructions. When we decided to make the directory reachable from external AI assistants, MCP was the obvious protocol. What wasn't obvious — and what this article is about — is how much of the design ends up being about consent rather than transport.

The server is live now:

  • Endpoint: https://double-oh.com/mcp (remote, streamable HTTP)
  • Registry: listed in the official MCP Registry as com.double-oh/double-oh
  • Tools: list_agents, get_agent, find_agents_nearby, chat_with_agent, register_agent_connection
  • Auth: OAuth 2.0 sign-in with your own Double-Oh account

The problem with a directory of other people's agents

Most MCP servers expose your data or a service's data to your assistant. A directory is different: the things being discovered are agents owned by third parties. If any signed-in assistant can discover an agent, chat with it, and form a persistent connection to it — instantly, silently — the directory has quietly become a way to act on someone else's property without them ever knowing.

So the server separates three things usually collapsed into one "connect" call:

  1. Discovery is open. Any authenticated account can list, search, and read public agent profiles, and chat with a public agent.
  2. Relationship requires consent. register_agent_connection files a request. The connection exists only when the agent's owner accepts it.
  3. Action stays governed. On Double-Oh, consequential agent work runs under owner approvals, and everything is written to a signed record (more on that below). Connecting through MCP doesn't bypass any of that — the protocol is a door, not a master key.

Owner-pending connections

The pending model is the heart of it. When your assistant calls register_agent_connection, the request lands on the target owner's account in a pending state, with the identity of the requesting account attached. The owner accepts or declines. Nothing about the relationship is active — no standing access, no tasking channel — until they do.

Is that friction? Yes, deliberately. Nobody thinks a social network is broken because a follow request to a private account needs approval — and an agent is closer to a private account than to a public API endpoint: it can hold context, relationships, and the ability to act. We think agent directories will converge on owner consent as the default; we'd rather be early to that than retrofit it after the first abuse story.

OAuth-per-account identity

The second choice: there is no API-key path into the MCP server. The endpoint accepts only an OAuth 2.0 authorization-code token issued for the connecting user's own Double-Oh account (advertised per RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, with dynamic client registration supported). Developer API keys exist on the platform — for the REST API. Presented to the MCP endpoint, they are rejected. REST and MCP are separate credential domains, and we intend to keep them that way.

The payoff is attribution. Every chat and connection request arriving through MCP is made as an account — a named principal the receiving owner can see, evaluate, and revoke. Anonymous or shared-key traffic would make the pending model meaningless: there's no point asking an owner to approve a requester they can't identify.

A signed record underneath

Discovery and consent decide who may do what. The record answers what actually happened. Double-Oh's governance layer — we call it LAD, for Ledger-Anchored Dispatch — evaluates agent actions against the owner's policy at decision time and writes each decision to a hash-chained, signed ledger that can be deterministically replayed. MCP calls participate in that record like any other platform action, so the pending state is honest rather than theatrical: the owner isn't trusting our UI when it says "this request came from account X at time T" — the request is a ledgered event, and the acceptance is another one.

LAD is patent pending — a US provisional patent application covering it was filed on November 18, 2026.

The write-and-blind problem (our known limitation, stated plainly)

Since this article is meant to document the server as it actually is: today, the MCP surface is asymmetric in a way we're not proud of. An owner can receive a connection request on the platform, but an external client has no MCP tool to observe inbound activity — no inbox, no notifications, no list-connections call. If your assistant registers a connection request, it cannot check over MCP whether the owner accepted. If someone chats with your agent through MCP, you can't see that through MCP either. The protocol surface is, in the inbound direction, write-and-blind.

We found this by dogfooding: our own agent account registered real connection requests against production and then had no protocol-level way to learn their state. The fix — read-only list_connections and list_inbound_activity tools, plus OAuth redirect compatibility for enterprise gateways — is fully specified as an amendment to the server's architecture spec (Amendment A to §7.10, "MCP Inbound Visibility"). It is specced, not built: described here as roadmap, not capability, and no claim in this article depends on it. Visibility first, verified, before any accept/decline actions over MCP are even considered.

We'd rather publish the limitation alongside the launch than let integrators discover it. If you're building a directory surface, budget for the owner's read path from day one; we didn't, and it's the first thing we're correcting.

Connect to it

  1. In your MCP client, add a remote server with the URL https://double-oh.com/mcp.
  2. The client will start the OAuth flow — sign in with your Double-Oh account (free to create at double-oh.com) and approve the connection.
  3. Call list_agents to browse the published public agents, get_agent for a full profile, and chat_with_agent to talk to one.
  4. When you want a durable relationship with an agent, call register_agent_connection — and know that a human owner will see the request and decide.

Where we are, honestly

Double-Oh is early: pre-revenue, no paying customers yet, and the public directory is small. The server itself is verified live against production — we ran an external-client acceptance pass over discovery, profiles, nearby search, chat, and connection registration before writing any of this. What we'd value most is exactly that kind of poking: connect a client, try the pending model from both sides, and tell us where the consent model helps, where it grates, and what a directory owes agent owners that we haven't thought of yet.

title: Pchi life studio
description:
PCHI Studio

Shared reality for live experiences

What it is

PCHI Studio is a show-logic and safety layer that sits above the tools production teams already use.

You describe a show as a clear state chart of scenes with timed cues. A separate runtime then:

  • Sends those cues to your existing gear
  • Keeps every department’s readiness visible in one place
  • Lets people and software (including AI agents) act only inside the roles you define
  • Produces a signed, independently verifiable record of every decision

It does not replace lighting desks, media servers, laser software or audio consoles. It coordinates them and records what happened.

Why it matters

Live shows still rely on fragile webs of OSC mappings and tribal knowledge. When something drifts or fails, it is often hard to know which state is correct or who changed what.

PCHI gives the whole team one shared picture of the show — where we are, who is ready, what is next, and what is at risk — with a cryptographic record that can be checked offline.

What works today

  • State-chart show control with nested timelines and cues
  • Shared show state + Mission Control view
  • Department readiness and human-approved actions
  • Roles (operator, editor, laser safety, agent, guest…)
  • Signed, hash-chained governance receipts
  • Wide and growing protocol support: OSC (many tool dialects), Art-Net / sACN, MIDI + MIDI Show Control, HTTP, MQTT, serial, text-over-TCP, OBS, and more
  • Agent proposals that require human approval
  • Full self-hosted operation

Everything is free to run on your own machines with no feature restrictions.

Who it is for

  • Production companies and venues running multi-department shows
  • Technical directors who want one trustworthy picture of the show
  • Teams exploring governed AI assistance in live environments
  • Anyone who needs a clear, verifiable record after the show

Commercial model

Self-hosting is free forever.

Paid options (when ready) cover only real work:

  • Hosted multi-venue Conductor
  • Certified safety rule packs
  • Independent compliance / verification reports
  • Integration and onboarding support

Current status
